item.title: Computational Exploration of Dopamine Adsorption on Carbon Nanotubes for Electrochemical Sensing
item.description: Dopamine (DA), has a variety of impacts on human health. Due to the high cost and labor-intensity of its current measurement methods, sensitive and low-cost electrochemical sensors with carbonaceous substrate materials have been proposed as an alternative. Single-chirality single-walled carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) have gained interest for their chirality-dependent properties. In a recent study, we demonstrated that the sensing response of DA varies for SWCNT chiralities. In this study, we performed density-functional theory (DFT) simulations to identify low-energy conformers of DA and to gain atomic-level understanding of the interactions upon DA adsorption on (6,6) SWCNTs. We utilized Bayesian Optimization Structure Search (BOSS) to sample energy landscapes and identify the lowest-energy DA conformers and adsorption configurations. As a result, we found 6 low-energy conformers of DA and one adsorption configuration type of DA on the (6,6) SWCNT, where the aromatic ring of DA adsorbs flat on the SWCNT and the flexible side chain is oriented away from the substrate. Analysis of its electronic structure revealed that DA physisorbs on the (6,6) SWCNT via the aromatic ring. The present workflow can be expanded to other chiralities and molecules to support substrate material development for electrochemical sensors with applications in healthcare and environmental monitoring.

item.title: Comparative Analysis of Basic Machine Learning and Rigorous Free-Energy Calculation on Benchmarking Datasets of Protein-Ligand Binding Affinity
item.description: Rigorous free-energy methods based on molecular dynamics simulations like free-energy perturbation (FEP) are nowadays widely applied in lead optimization in pharmaceutical companies. Due to sampling restrictions and potential force-field deficiencies, it is common practice to first validate the applicability of FEP to a target/chemical series using a small number of known compounds, before applying it prospectively. As rigorous methods require significant computational resources, we want to explore how basic machine learning (ML) methods perform under the same conditions, i.e., training on a small number of known compounds and estimating the affinity of novel variants in the same chemical series. We apply classical ML models using 2D and 3D molecular descriptors, alongside two implementations of 3D quantitative structure–activity relationship modeling, and integrate the predictions through meta-learning. For many of the standard benchmarking datasets, we find that one of the ML models matches or exceeds the performance of FEP. Interestingly, ML-based predictions generally exhibit flatter slopes in parity plots, but without substantial effect on the relative rank ordering of compounds. Given their lower computational cost and ease of deployment, basic ML methods, particularly the meta-learner, emerge as a powerful complement to rigorous free-energy methods for estimating binding affinities within chemical series.

item.title: Dynamics of oxygen and hydrogen species at the surface Ru/Al2O3 revealed by advanced operando spectroscopies
item.description: The microscopic evolution of supported Ru-oxide nanoparticles under reducing conditions remains a central challenge in hydrogenation catalysis. In 5 wt% Ru/Al2O3 catalyst, the transformation of oxidized Ru species into metallic Ru, the formation of hydrides, and hydrogen exchange with the support are closely related but difficult to resolve simultaneously. Here, operando IR and O K-edge NEXAFS, supported by quantum chemical DFT calculations, show that the initially hydroxylated Ru-oxide surface contains *OOH and *OO-H species at unsaturated Ru sites characterized by a distinct O K-edge electronic signature. Upon dehydration, removal of neighboring surface groups strongly stabilizes a bridged η2-peroxo species with a characteristic vibrational fingerprint. Subsequent exposure to H2 drives a low-temperature multistep reduction to metallic Ru and leads to the transient formation of terminal Ru–H species. Inelastic neutron scattering (INS) measurements independently reveal multi-coordinated hydrides under hydrogen-rich conditions, while H/D isotope exchange shows reversible hydrogen exchange between Ru nanoparticles and the support. The concomitant recovery of alumina hydroxyl groups upon H2 exposure further supports hydrogen transfer to the support. These results provide insight on the evolution of the catalyst, showing that surface dehydroxylation, Ru-oxide reduction, hydride formation, and hydrogen transfer are closely connected during activation of Ru/Al2O3 catalysts.

Dataset-specific retention time adjustment and multi-evidence lipid annotation: a reproducible R workflow for untargeted LC–MS lipidomics
item.description: Background and Objective: Untargeted lipid annotation by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry is challenged by structural isomers, multiple ion forms, and retention time differences between analytical datasets. We developed an open-source computational workflow combining dataset-specific retention time adjustment with experimentally characterized lipid information to restrict candidate assignments while preserving unresolved identities. Methods: The R workflow uses a curated database of 592 lipid species derived from a human plasma reference material. It combines monotonic retention time adjustment, accurate-mass matching, isotope-pattern assessment, empirical adduct profile, and ambiguity resolution. Developed using a 40-sample MICROSAMPLING study, it was applied to an independent 189-sample METFORMIN-HIIE study acquired under compatible chromatographic conditions. Annotation stages were evaluated against fixed workflow-derived references, including a comparison with unadjusted database retention times. Results: Unadjusted retention time matching recovered 55.4-77.2% of reference feature-lipid pairs, whereas adjusted matching recovered all reference pairs under identical tolerances. RT adjustment reduced candidates on non-reference features by 69.5-83.2% relative to mass-only matching and increased within-reference candidate discrimination from 69.1-70.9% to 88.5-92.6%. Isotope filtering and ambiguity resolution further restricted assignments. Integration across ionization modes yielded 433 and 379 endogenous feature records, respectively; 93 and 100 retained multiple compatible lipid identities rather than forcing unsupported unique assignments. Conclusions: Dataset-specific adjustment improves agreement with workflow-curated assignments while restricting candidate space. The approach supports reproducible lipid annotation and transparent uncertainty handling. Because the reference assignments originate from the workflow itself, complete retention does not establish independent annotation sensitivity or accuracy.

item.title: Anisotropic Strain Enhances Oxygen Reduction Catalysis in Pt-Based High-Entropy Intermetallics
item.description: The oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) remains a major bottleneck for the efficiency of proton exchange membrane fuel cells. While alloying Pt with 3d transition metals can reduce Pt loading and improve catalytic activity of ORR catalysts, Pt-based solid solutions suffer from reduced activity and stability at Pt fractions below 75-80 at. %. Here, we investigate the role of atomic ordering in multimetallic Pt catalysts by comparing high-entropy solid solutions (HESOSO) and high-entropy intermetallics (HEI) with identical nominal composition, Pt5MnFeCoNiCu. Gas diffusion electrode (GDE) setup measurements at industrially relevant current densities (>1 A cm-2 geo) show that catalysts containing the intermetallic phase outperform solid solution counterparts in both specific and mass activity despite their larger particle sizes. Density functional theory calculations attribute this improvement to anisotropic strain arising from the tetragonal intermetallic lattice, which generates distinct adsorption environments with near-optimal *OH binding energies. These results identify strain anisotropy in ordered multimetallic intermetallics as a promising catalyst design principle for independently tuning adsorption energetics and Pt loading. On-line inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) measurements reveal reduced 3d-metal dissolution in the HEI sample compared to HESOSO sample and binary PtNi reference. Operando X-ray total scattering and pair distribution function analysis further demonstrate that both crystallographic structure and local atomic arrangement are retained during accelerated stress testing, indicating that nanoparticle structural collapse is not the dominant degradation pathway. Instead, the observed activity losses are primarily associated with catalyst-layer degradation and mass transport limitations. Overall, the results identify atomic ordering and strain anisotropy as key parameters for designing low-Pt ORR catalysts with enhanced activity and structural stability under operating conditions.

item.title: Breaking Linear Scaling Relations for Regioselective Phenol Hydroxylation via SiC-Supported Dual-Atom Catalysts
item.description: The electrochemical hydroxylation of phenol offers a sustainable route to valueadded dihydroxybenzene isomers, yet rational catalyst design remains limited by 2 poor regioselectivity and structural instability. This study investigates silicon carbide (SiC) monoliths as exceptionally robust supports for dual-atom catalysts, utilizing density functional theory and operando ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) to screen 45 bimetallic combinations. Mechanistic analysis reveals that phenol undergoes site-specific activation directly at the Si-lattice, dictating regioselectivity toward catechol (ortho-pathway) or hydroquinone (para-pathway). Crystal Orbital Hamilton Population analyses and energetic span modeling demonstrate that macroscopic turnover is strictly governed by dynamic orbital overlap and precise d-band alignment. The TiFe configuration optimally minimizes the energetic span for ortho-hydroxylation, while TiMn provide the most competitive pathways for para-hydroxylation. Two-dimensional microkinetic mapping confirms that optimizing surface binding thermodynamics and bimetallic electronics successfully circumvents traditional linear scaling relations. Furthermore, operando AIMD simulations at 298 K validate these models, confirming that aromatic 𝜋-electron disruption constitutes the kinetic bottleneck (0.70 eV) and highlighting the critical role of interfacial potassium cations in electrostatically shielding polarized radical transition states.

item.title: Spatial Inhomogeneity of Thermal Degradation of Semi-Crystalline Polymers
item.description: The thermal degradation of polymers is typically interpreted as a uniform chemical process involving molecular weight reduction and oxidation. However, the role of localized microstructural changes as defect sites that deteriorate polymer mechanical performance remains underexplored owing to the limitations of conventional bulk characterization techniques. We applied an isotope-labeled Raman mapping technique with molecular weight selectivity to visualize the structural evolution of semi-crystalline polyethylene during long-term thermal exposure under conditions in which the bulk molecular weight and carbonyl index remained nearly unchanged. In this material, mechanical deterioration is induced by spatially localized structural changes. Despite the negligible average chemical change, the ductility decreased drastically upon heating. High-resolution mapping revealed discrete domains of enhanced crystallinity and conformational ordering, which emerged with spherulite-scale correlation lengths that expanded with the aging time. These domains spatially coincide with the fracture-origin regions after tensile deformation. Molecular weight-resolved analysis showed that high-molecular-weight chains preferentially underwent degradation-induced crystallization (chemi-crystallization), suggesting that regions rich in tie molecules are the primary transformation sites. Our findings show that thermal exposure is a defect nucleation process governed by structural heterogeneity, providing a new framework for predicting the long-term reliability of semi-crystalline polymers. This mechanism provides a predictive foundation for a wide range of engineering thermoplastics.

item.title: Benchmarking a fast energy model for predicting the stability of solvated surface sites for organic molecular crystals: The paracetamol–water interface
item.description: Crystallisation of molecular materials is important for a range of industries including the pharmaceutical and agrochemical sectors. Prediction of the crystal growth and dissolution of such systems requires detailed knowledge of the thermodynamics, and ideally kinetics, of surface sites in contact with solvent. The most reliable method for obtaining the free energy of solvated kinks, step edges and terraces with molecular resolution is often via computer simulation using molecular dynamics, as this includes explicit solvent interactions and entropy changes, but comes at a significant computational cost. Here this approach is used to provide a series of benchmark standard free energies for dissolution of different types of surface sites at the paracetamol form I (001) interface with water. A modified GAFF force field is used that is calibrated to predict the solubility of paracetamol in good agreement with experiment. These reference free energies are then used to examine the accuracy of a faster, more approximate method that has been previously tested primarily for solubility and morphology prediction, namely the CrystalClear protocol. Results show that not only do both approaches have the same qualitative trends, with removal of the first molecule from the terrace at the aqueous interface having a significantly higher thermodynamic cost relative to removal from kink sites, but both approaches are in quantitative agreement to within the uncertainty of the molecular dynamics results for nearly all surface sites. The only site that exhibits a noticeable difference is for the removal of the final molecule from a step and occurs due to relaxation effects. The excellent agreement between the two methods examined here provides confidence that the CrystalClear approach represents a reliable and efficient means of predicting the thermodynamic stability of individual molecular binding sites at solvated interfaces, which can then be used for coarse-grained methods such as Monte Carlo simulation of crystal growth and dissolution.

item.title: Enhancing Interfacial Exciton Conversion in Blue Upconversion OLEDs through Oligomer-Controlled Molecular Orientation
item.description: Controlling molecular orientation is central to high-performance organic optoelectronics. Anthracene oligomers provide an orientation-tunable platform for elucidating orientation effects in upconversion organic light-emitting diodes (UC-OLEDs), which generate blue emission at exceptionally low driving voltages through interfacial charge-transfer (CT) states, CT-to-triplet (CT-to-T1) conversion, and triplet–triplet annihilation. Across anthracene derivatives, increasing horizontal orientation enhances external quantum efficiency (EQE) beyond that expected from light outcoupling alone. To identify the underlying processes, the randomly oriented monomer 1,2-ADN and the preferentially horizontally oriented dimer p-ADN-1 serve as representatives. Both interface-exchanged devices, in which interfacial and emitting-layer anthracene species are varied independently, and transient absorption measurements consistently show that horizontal orientation enhances interfacial CT-to-T1 conversion. Overall, a more horizontal orientation of the host molecules improves light outcoupling by only ~4% but enhances interfacial CT-to-T1 conversion efficiency by 1.3–1.5-fold. Beyond its ultralow turn-on voltage of 1.5 V, the optimized p-ADN-1 device achieves an EQE of 2.61%, a 1.5-fold improvement over the 1,2-ADN device, and a LT50 (time to 50% of the initial luminance) exceeding 1750 h at 1000 cd m−2. To our knowledge, these values represent the highest EQE and longest operational lifetime reported for blue OLEDs with turn-on voltages below 2 V. These findings establish molecular orientation as an active structural parameter governing both light outcoupling and interfacial exciton conversion.

item.title: Helicene-Blade Molecular Propellers
item.description: Molecular propellers have attracted intense interest as a fascinating class of chiral molecules, as exemplified by hexaphenylbenzene derivatives bearing peripheral point-chiral substituents. However, these molecules typically show limited chiral configuration stability, hindering applications that require stable chiroptical responses. Herein, helicenes are introduced as blades to construct molecular propellers for the first time, achieving enhanced chiral stability. A stereospecific synthesis from enantiopure aza[7]helicene (A7H) is employed to obtain a propeller-shaped A7H hexamer (HA7H), which shows a high critical temperature (Tc) of 23 °C for chiral inversion. Such a high Tc sets a new record among molecular propellers (typically from –50 to 10 °C), highlighting the advantage of helicenes as blades for acquiring configurationally stable molecular propellers.

item.title: Beyond Atom Pairs: Multicenter Crystal Orbital Hamilton Populations for Molecules and Solids
item.description: The Crystal Orbital Hamilton Population (COHP) is a standard tool for energyresolved bonding analysis in solids and also applies to molecules, but it assigns the band energy only to atom pairs. A multicenter bond therefore has no energy of its own: across the five molecules and solids studied here, pairwise integrated COHP reports strong two-center bonding (−1.8 to −3.5 eV) and cannot distinguish an electrondeficient bridge from an electron-rich unit. item.title: Targeted Covalent Inhibition of Pyk2 via a Paralog-Specific Cysteine for Selective Antiplatelet Action
item.description: Focal adhesion kinase 2 (FAK2, also known as Pyk2), a focal adhesion kinase (FAK) family member, has emerged as a promising antiplatelet target with minimal impact on normal hemostasis. However, the development of Pyk2-selective inhibitors has been constrained by limited paralog selectivity and suboptimal in vivo pharmacokinetics. Here, we report compound 2-1, a first-in-class covalent inhibitor that selectively targets Pyk2 by hijacking a unique cysteine residue (Cys545) absent in the sister kinase FAK1. Using structure-guided design, we modified the reversible inhibitor PF-4594755 with an acrylamide electrophile and a methylazetidine spacer to enable covalent engagement of Cys545. Intracellular NanoBRET assays and an alkyne-tagged analogue of 2-1 validated its covalent mechanism and kinome-wide selectivity. Functionally, 2-1 impaired platelet responses to the thromboxane A2 analog U46619, while showing moderate-to-minimal effects on adenosine diphosphate- and thrombin-induced aggregation. Under microfluidic simulated arterial and venous flow conditions in human whole blood, 2-1 reduced platelet adhesion comparably to aspirin. In an electrolytic carotid artery thrombosis model, 2-1 tripled the thrombolytic efficacy of recombinant tissue plasminogen activator without increasing bleeding risks. This work provides a foundation for the development of selective Pyk2 inhibitors as a new class of safe, bleeding-sparing antiplatelets for thrombotic disorders.

item.title: Transfer learning on universal interatomic potential embeddings improves generalization in structure-property defect models
item.description: Oxygen vacancy formation energies govern the performance of metal oxides across energy conversion, catalysis, and electronics, yet predicting them accurately without density functional theory calculations for novel chemical systems remains challenging. Here, we show that frozen 256-dimensional embeddings extracted from a pretrained MACE universal machine-learning interatomic potential encode information sufficient to predict vacancy formation energies obtained from density functional theory without requiring supercell construction, vacancy creation, or geometry optimization. A lightweight multilayer perceptron trained on these embeddings (MACE-dGNN) achieves an element-wise cross-validation mean absolute error of 0.38 eV, halving the error of a baseline graph neural network trained from scratch (0.72 eV) and offering a modest advantage over direct MACE relaxation calculations (0.51 eV). Because the embedding approach decouples representation from the prediction task and generalizes well with limited data, it will (1) extend naturally to fine-tuning and prediction of properties (e.g., charged defects) that are inaccessible to generic energy-and force-output interatomic potentials and (2) be trainable on necessarily small datasets, potentially enabling the use of more expensive but accurate tools for generating training data (e.g., hybrid functional calculations) for which training or fine-tuning of interatomic potentials will be difficult. We demonstrate practical impact by revisiting a prior screening of thermochemical water-splitting materials, where improved generalization alters ∼45 % of candidate classifications.

item.title: Data-driven discovery and substrate scope mapping of dual-ligand nickel catalysts for C(sp2)–C(sp3) cross-electrophile coupling
item.description: Dual-ligand nickel catalysis has emerged as an effective strategy for improving C(sp2)–C(sp3) cross-electrophile coupling (XEC), yet the systematic studies identifying productive ligand combinations and mapping their target scope remain limited. In this work, we combine high-throughput experimentation (HTE) with a simple, interpretable data-analysis workflow to identify and validate synergistic bidentate–tridentate ligand pairs for Zn-mediated Ni-catalyzed XEC. An HTE screening campaign spanning nine model reactions and 77 ligand combinations per plate enabled simultaneous evaluation of performance, robustness, and non-additive behavior of the catalytic systems. Statistical analysis revealed six ligand pairs that combined strong overall activity with measurable positive synergy, including combinations related to previously reported systems as well as new productive pairings. Using a diverse panel of 96 pharmaceutically relevant (hetero)aryl bromides, we demonstrated that dual-ligand systems often outperformed the best single ligand and could cover the studied substrate space more efficiently. Critically, for certain dual-ligand catalysts, these benefits tracked with interpretable electronic descriptors, providing a practical basis for prioritizing which substrate classes are most likely to profit from the usage of ligand pairs. Together, these results demonstrate that HTE coupled with lightweight statistical analysis provides an efficient route to the discovery of complex catalytic systems, their prioritization and mapping their scope. Our findings also establish dual-ligand Ni catalysis as a practical strategy for expanding the scope and increasing the success rate of thermally driven XEC relevant to pharmaceutical synthesis.

item.title: Controlled Competition Reduces Errors in Nanostructure-Based DNA Data Storage
item.description: DNA nanotechnology offers a promising route toward molecular data storage with exceptional density, longevity, and energy efficiency. Unlike sequence-based approaches that rely on large-scale synthesis and sequencing, structural DNA data storage encodes information into spatial architectures readable at the single-molecule level. However, practical implementation is hindered by substitution errors -particularly 0-to-1 “bit flips” - that arise during pooled readout and compromise data fidelity. Here, we introduce and systematically benchmark a set of thermodynamically-tuned error protection strategies for DNA ‘hard drive’ nanostructures, based on controlled competition between a label strand and a protector strand. By rationally modulating hybridisation stability through toehold truncation, internal mismatches, or self-complementary clamping, we identify a protector strand with a single cytosine-thymine (C-T) mismatch as an optimal design. This straightforward modification yields >90% readout fidelity and increases the information-theoretic channel capacity 25-fold relative to unprotected overhangs. The 1 C–T mismatch protector will enable accurate data writing and pooled readout using solid-state nanopore sensing, demonstrating scalable, high-fidelity molecular data retrieval. Overall, our findings establish new design principles for error suppression in structural DNA data storage and represent a key step toward practical, sustainable molecular information technologies.

item.title: Revisiting Artifact Suppression in Electrospray Ionization Deconvolution
item.description: Charge state assignment is a critical step in many workflows for intact protein analysis by mass spectrometry. Computational deconvolution algorithms are increasingly used to automate data analysis, but conventional approaches can present artifacts. Here, we explore several approaches to remove artifacts by limiting the charge state assignments for each data point. One approach removes satellite charge states surrounding local maxima. Another removes harmonics at double a more probable charge assignment. The last two limit either the total number of allowed charge state assignments or the minimum relative charge state assignment probability for a given data point. These new features are as effective as the prior SoftMax artifact removal in UniDec, but they enable easier tuning by the user. Although the new set of features introduces additional complexity and an expanded number of parameters, these tools enable users to more precisely reduce artifacts in deconvolution results.

item.title: Tailoring Pt-CeO2 Interactions to Bypass Activity-Selectivity Trade-Off for C2H2 Semi-Hydrogenation
item.description: CeO2-supported platinum-group metals with small nanoparticles allow fine-tuning of their electronic properties through enhanced electronic interactions with the support. Here, we modify the electronic properties of a Pt/CeO2 catalyst with 1.5 nm Pt nanoparticles by varying the near-surface oxygen vacancy concentration. In-situ infrared, X-ray photoelectron, and X-ray absorption spectroscopies show that roomtemperature oxidation followed by re-reduction at 100 oC decreases near-surface oxygen vacancies by ∼3-fold without altering Pt size, resulting in ∼25-fold increase in C2H2 hydrogenation turnover frequency while C2H4 selectivity remains unchanged at ∼90%. These findings are exceptional for C2H2 semi-hydrogenation since C2H4 selectivity typically decreases with increasing C2H2 activity due to the well-known linear scaling relationship and Brønsted-Evans-Polanyi relation. X-ray absorption spectroscopy and density functional theory calculations reveal that lowering subsurface oxygen vacancy concentration unevenly depletes Pt d-electron density, altering projected density of states exclusively for apex Pt sites. Competitive adsorption modeling reveals that apex Pt sites preferentially adsorb C2H2, while basal Pt sites favor C2H4, leading to a stronger effect on C2H2 binding and resulting in the observed deviation from the typical activity-selectivity trade-off. Our study demonstrates that tailoring Pt-CeO2 interactions enables site- and molecule-specific adsorption modulation to overcome the conventional activity–selectivity trade-off.

item.title: Machine Learning for NMR Observables Sensitive to Nuclear Quantum Effects
item.description: Nuclear quantum effects (NQEs) are essential for an accurate description of systems containing light elements. Their omission in classical simulations can lead to significant deviations between theoretical predictions and experimental measurements, particularly for nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) observables that are highly sensitive to quantum nuclear motion. Although NQEs can be treated rigorously by using ab initio path-integral molecular dynamics (AI-PIMD), the substantial computational cost associated with these simulations continues to limit their applicability to large systems and long timescales. To address this limitation, we developed a machine learning-driven PIMD (MLPIMD) workflow for the accurate and efficient prediction of NMR observables, in which NQEs at finite temperature are explicitly included. As a demonstration, we investigate the experimentally measured isotropic chemical shifts, δiso, of the 3He monomer (3He@C706- ) and dimer (3He2@C706- ) endohedral fullerene hexaanions. The resulting predictions show excellent agreement with the experiment and reveal a pronounced influence of NQEs on the 3He chemical shifts in both systems. In particular, NQEs are found to play a key role in determining the chemical-shift difference between the monomer and dimer species. The methodology introduced here is broadly applicable and provides a general framework for investigating NMR observables sensitive to NQEs in complex molecular systems.

item.title: Intramolecular Hydride Migration Enables Ring Substitution in a Diphosphacyclobutadienyl Complex
item.description: While substitution reactions at coordinated carbocyclic π-ligands are well established, similar examples of direct substitution at the ring carbon atoms of mixed carbon-phosphorus π-systems have remained scarce, owing to the intrinsic bias towards P-centered reactivity. Herein, we report a hydride-for-phosphonium substitution at a coordinated phosphorus heterocyclic π-system: protonation of the complex [W(CO)3{η 4-(PPh3)2C2P2}] bearing a zwitterionic diphosphacyclobutadienyl ligand affords a tungsten hydride complex which undergoes a selective rearrangement to [W(CO)3(PPh3){η 4-(PPh3)HC2P2}][OTf] upon dissolution in acetonitrile. A combined experimental and computational investigation reveals a multistep pathway, in which a tungsten-mediated intramolecular hydride migration serves as the key step. Acetonitrile plays a crucial role in driving the reaction by stabilizing the coordinatively unsaturated intermediate generated upon hydride migration. Remarkably, despite its negative charge, the resulting phosphonium-hydro-diphosphete-diide ligand combines strong π-donor and pronounced π-acceptor properties, resulting in stronger binding to the tungsten carbonyl fragment than the cyclopentadienyl ligand, as evidenced by EDANOCV calculations and IR spectroscopy.

item.title: Computer-Guided In-situ Screening of Poly(acetylene)s for Gene Delivery
item.description: We report a new methodology for the discovery of polymer-based gene vectors that enables the simultaneous optimization of polymer composition and polyplex formulation, while bypassing the need to prepare, isolate, and characterise new candidates using conventional polymer synthesis. At the core of this approach is the combination of computer-aided experimental design, in situ screening of polymer composition and polyplex formulation, and machine learning, which allows us to treat polymer synthesis and formulation as a single optimizable problem. Central to this methodology is a new reactive and water-soluble poly(acetylene), poly(N-(propargyl)-2-(aminooxy)-acetamide), which can be functionalized in aqueous conditions with readily available aldehydes. This provides candidate polymers under biologically compatible conditions, which are then directly complexed with nucleic acids and evaluated within the same workflow. Iterative modelling then correlates inputs readily controlled by the operator—such as reagent concentrations and ratios—with the key performance metric, transfection efficiency, guiding subsequent rounds of candidate generation. In doing so, we move beyond post hoc correlations of physicochemical properties to establish an iterative, data-driven methodology for materials discovery. Ultimately, this methodology has unlocked the potential of poly(acetylene)s, a polymer family not previously explored in this context, to move beyond compositional mimicry and capture the dynamic helicity that underpins nucleic acid complexation and delivery in natural systems.

item.title: The infinitesimal machine surgeon: prospects for upconversion nanoparticles driving molecular motors/nanomachines
item.description: The concept of the “infinitesimal machine surgeon” was envisaged by Feynman in 1959 and 1983, describing a miniature, human-controllable machine capable of being directed to biological tissue to perform a physical intervention. This perspective explores the potential of combining Feringa-type rotary molecular motors (nanomachines) with upconversion nanoparticles (UCNPs) to realise the vision of the infinitesimal machine surgeon. In this approach, UCNPs convert near-infrared (NIR) excitation into ultraviolet/visible (UV/Vis) emission to activate molecular nanomachines within biological tissue. The fundamental operating principles are outlined, recent experimental advances in powering molecular motors and UCNPs in organic solvents are reviewed. Simple biophotonic calculations based on the Beer–Lambert law suggest that upconversion from 808 nm to 450–475 nm may offer a promising excitation strategy for activating molecular motors in biological tissues. Key challenges to biological implementation are identified, including permissible tissue light-exposure levels and the effects of tissue absorption and multiple scattering on the photon budget available to drive UCNPs and molecular motors. Finally, experimental strategies for evaluating these systems in biologically relevant environments are proposed, in accordance with the 3Rs principles of biomedical research.

item.title: From Azirinyl Radicals to Azirinium Cations: Small-Ring N-Heterocyclic Reactive Intermediates
item.description: Late-stage functionalization via reactive intermediates has recently emerged as an efficient way to access structurally diverse small rings, as illustrated with cyclopropyl radicals or cyclopropenium cations, which have opened valuable new synthetic opportunities. Their nitrogen counterparts, however, remain underexplored despite the importance of heterocycles in synthetic and medicinal chemistry. Herein, we demonstrate that azirinyl radicals and azirinium cations can be reliably accessed from a common N-hydroxyphthalimide ester azirine precursor under blue light irradiation, without the need for a metal catalyst. Under reductive conditions, azirinyl radicals can be added to electron-poor alkenes and using a radical polar-crossover approach, azirinium cations can be trapped with nucleophiles. Both pathways are high-yielding, chemically robust and scalable to give azirines with a wide range of substituents previously inaccessible and can be applied to complex drug-derived molecules. The obtained azirines could be converted to the corresponding aziridines diastereoselectively.

item.title: Cobalt-Catalyzed Dual Construction of peri-(C–C) and (C–N)/(N–N) Atropisomerism via C–H Activation
item.description: Axially chiral biaryls bearing an atropisomeric C–C axis at peri-substituted positions are difficult to access, and this difficulty compounds when the same scaffold must also carry a second, independent C–N or N–N axis, a combination that remains largely unexplored. Here we report an efficient, cost-effective route to these dual-axial atropisomers through enantioselective Co(II)/Salox-catalyzed C–H/N–H annulation. Arylbenzamide substrates bearing two distinct classes of directing groups react with peri-substituted alkynes to install both stereogenic axes in a single step. The reaction tolerates a broad range of substituents, proceeds in good yield, and delivers excellent stereocontrol (up to >99% ee, >20:1 dr). Mechanistic studies, supported by density functional theory (DFT) calculations, clarify the origin of the observed stereoselectivity. The resulting dual-axial atropisomers are fluorescent, and their photophysical properties point to potential applications in optoelectronic materials.

item.title: Antisolvent precipitation of Zinc Porphyrin Hydrogen-Bonded Organic Frameworks Enables J-Aggregation Mediated Electrochemiluminescence for Synthetic Cannabinoid Sensing
item.description: Zinc porphyrin hydrogen-bonded organic frameworks (ZnTCPP HOFs) represent attractive electrochemiluminescence (ECL) luminophores; however, their tendency to undergo uncontrolled short-range π–π stacking at solid/liquid interfaces induces aggregation-caused quenching (ACQ) and severely limits the ECL efficiency. Existing strategies for suppressing ACQ rely mainly on covalent or coordination-mediated ligand engineering and often require laborious multi-step synthesis. From the perspective of colloid and interface science, we herein report a chitosan (CS)–DMF antisolvent precipitation strategy that reorganizes the interfacial hydrogen-bond network between CS and the carboxyl groups of ZnTCPP HOFs, enabling a controlled transformation of bulk crystals into short-range aggregates with local J-type coupling. Such synergistic colloidal-interface regulation suppresses short-range π–π stacking while enabling J-aggregates to enhance the ECL emission, boosting the peak ECL intensity without the need for an additional co-reaction promoter. On this basis, an aptamer-based ECL sensor was constructed for the ultrasensitive detection of the synthetic cannabinoid 5F-EDMB-PINACA, achieving a limit of detection of 8.61 × 10⁻16 g/L together with satisfactory selectivity and reliable determination in e-cigarette liquid samples. These findings demonstrate that colloidal-interface regulation provides an efficient and synthesis-free route toward high-performance ECL sensing.

item.title: Gold deposition on surfaces using small organic molecules: effects of preparation conditions on morphology and Raman response
item.description: Reduction and subsequent deposition of noble metals from simple salt solutions on solid surfaces remains challenging. We describe deposition of gold (nano)-particles from an aqueous chloroauric adic solution on glass and polyethylene surfaces at ambient temperature by adding simple primordial organic molecules. The deposited gold structures showed differences in morphology, size and Raman response across the preparation conditions examined, motivating further investigation of their potential as functional surface coatings with distinct properties for various applications. Green foundation 1 This work examines gold deposition on glass and plastic, hydrophobic and hydrophilic, surfaces using aqueous solutions of simple organic compounds at room temperature; mild reaction conditions relevant to green chemistry. 2 Light and electron microscopy revealed differences in deposit morphology across conditions with different organic compounds and reagent concentrations. 3 Cancer cell and rhodamine 6G Raman measurements were used to explore the potential of the deposited gold structures as substrates for surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy to detect biofilm compounds.

item.title: Chemical Synthesis and Immunological Evaluation of Archaeal Rare Sugar L-TalNAcA and Its Derivatives
item.description: Human-associated archaea, such as Methanobrevibacter smithii and Methanosphaera stadtmanae, have attracted increasing attention for their potential involvement in the modulation of host immune responses. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying these interactions remain poorly understood. Pseudopeptidoglycan (pPG), a major component of the archaeal cell wall, is a potential mediator of such immunomodulatory effects. Although N-acetyl-L-talosaminuronic acid (L-TalNAcA) has been proposed as a constituent of pPG, both its precise structural context within the archaeal cell wall and the immunological properties of its glycoconjugates remain largely unexplored. In this study, we established a synthetic route to L-TalNAcA and its derivatives, including mono- and disaccharide glycopeptides. LC-MS/MS analysis using synthetic L-TalNAcA as a reference standard supported the presence of this rare sugar in archaeal cell wall hydrolysates. Furthermore, immunological evaluation using reporter cell lines revealed that the M. smithii-type monosaccharide glycopeptide induced hNOD2-dependent activation. These findings provide molecular evidence of host receptor recognition of an archaeal cell wall-related glycopeptide motif and establish a chemical platform for further investigating archaeal-host immune interactions.

item.title: Adaptive Hydration-Shell ML/MM Simulations Recover Full ML Accuracy in Biomolecular Conformational Description
item.description: Residue-specific backbone conformational preferences govern the conformational ensembles of intrinsically disordered proteins, yet their accurate description using classical force fields is limited by prescribed functional forms that cannot fully represent environment-dependent many-body interactions. Machine-learned force fields (MLFFs) learn complex atomic interactions directly from quantum-mechanical reference data, providing a systematic alternative to classical parameterisations. Here, we employ a pretrained MLFF to simulate nine cationic Gly-x-Gly tripeptides in water and compare the resulting conformational ensembles against experimental NMR scalar J-couplings. To improve computational efficiency, we develop and assess hybrid Machine Learning/Molecular Mechanics (ML/MM) protocols as computationally tractable alternatives to full ML simulation. Mechanical-embedding ML/MM is found insufficient for accurate conformational sampling, as the classical treatment of peptide–solvent interactions fails to adequately represent solvation effects on backbone conformational preferences. We therefore implement an adaptive ML/MM scheme that incorporates the immediate solvation environment into the ML description and recovers near-full-ML accuracy at a reduced computational cost.

item.title: Tight binding of optically innocent bisphosphonate ligands to robust Tb3+-doped HfO2 nanocrystal surfaces
item.description: Lanthanide (Ln3+)-doped nanocrystals feature photostable, long-lived emission, making them attractive probes for in vitro and in vivo imaging. Their translation, however, hinges on a surface chemistry that confers colloidal stability under physiological conditions without compromising their photophysical properties. Here, we benchmark three classes of PEGylated anchoring groups—nitrocatecholates, phosphonates and bisphosphonates—on core and core/shell Tb3+-doped HfO2 nanocrystals. Nitrodopamine-based ligands quench Tb3+ luminescence in water on both core and core/shell particles, whereas phosphonic and bisphosphonic acids are optically innocent and leave the emission intact. Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) and dynamic light scattering (DLS) reveal that only the bisphosphonates remain tightly bound and keep the nanocrystals dispersed across a wide pH range and in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS). Nanocrystals capped with PEGylated bisphosphonate (bisPA−PEG250) retain their luminescence after prolonged incubation in PBS, with no detectable Hf or Tb leaching. Thus, PEGylated bisphosphonates emerge as robust, non-perturbing ligands for Ln3+-doped HfO2 and as a practical entry point to biomedical application, since Tb3+-doped HfO2 can be used as probes in bio-imaging of leukemia cells.

item.title: Automated Full-Spectrum Multivariate Calibration for Quantitative Glow Discharge Optical Emission Spectrometry
item.description: Glow discharge optical emission spectrometry (GD-OES) enables rapid bulk and depthresolved multi-elemental analysis of solid materials with minimal sample preparation. Conventional quantification, however, relies on preselected analyte emission lines and, if sputtering-rate variations must be compensated, on matrix reference lines or sputtering-rate correction, requiring matrix composition or sputtering rates as input. Modern CCD-based instruments simultaneously record broadband spectra containing thousands of spectral variables, yet most of this information remains unused in conventional calibration based on a few selected lines. Here, we investigate a full-spectrum calibration strategy based on Variable Importance in Projection-selected Partial Least Squares (VIP-PLS) regression for the quantitative determination of individual alloying elements. Al-Si and Cu-Zn alloys were selected as metallurgically and spectrochemically distinct model systems, with Si and Zn as target analytes, respectively. The VIP-PLS models predicted Si and Zn with Root Mean Square Error of Cross-Validation (RMSECV) values of 0.38 wt% and 0.50 wt%, compared with 1.05 wt% and 1.41 wt% for univariate calibration of a single preselected line, and 0.24 wt% and 0.63 wt% for normalized ratio-based calibration using a reference line and the matrix mass fraction. VIP-PLS thus achieved performance comparable to the ratio-based calibration, implicitly compensating for sample-specific intensity variations, such as the sputtering rate, without matrix composition as input and without manual line selection. Time-resolved evaluation further showed that model performance reflects the transient and steady-state stages of the glow discharge, while VIP analysis revealed which spectral features contribute most strongly to the calibration and how they evolve during sputtering. Full-spectrum multivariate calibration therefore provides an automated, spectrum-driven and interpretable route for matrix-specific quantitative GD-OES that exploits information already contained in broadband measurements.

item.title: SandCat: OpenMM Framework for Prospective Cryptic Pocket Discovery
item.description: Proteins are dynamic biomolecules, yet often in drug discovery they are treated as static entities. A relevant example of this are cryptic pockets, which are pockets that are not present in the apo structure but reveal themselves upon binding to a particular ligand. Methods based on molecular dynamics (MD) simulations can dynamically probe the protein structure and have been validated on known cryptic pocket sites. SWISH-X is one of the most prominent methods in this field. Previously, it was only available with GROMACS and PLUMED, which limited its speed. Here, we present SandCat, an OpenMM-based toolkit that implements this enhanced sampling method for cryptic pocket discovery. SandCat reproduces previous results from SWISH-X with twice the computational speed. Furthermore, SandCat provides standardised protocols for prospective use on targets where cryptic pockets are not known. We tested the SandCat pipeline on challenging targets, and recovered every characterised cryptic site within the top six candidate sites, with no sites detected for a negative control. We believe that the increased speed and the implementation of a prospective toolkit will enable SandCat to be used at scale to unlock previously undruggable targets.

item.title: A Pharmacophore-Based Virtual Screening Approach for the Discovery of Novel P2Y12 Receptor Ligands
item.description: Microglia play key roles in neuroinflammation, which is a hallmark of neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson’s disease, Alzheimer’s disease and Multiple Sclerosis. To strengthen our understanding of the molecular mechanisms of these disorders, we need to understand the complex dynamics in microglial states. Developing new positron emission tomography (PET) tracers is exceptionally useful for this purpose, as they enable the assessment of microglia dynamics and function in the living human brain. The purinergic receptor P2Y12 (P2Y12R) is highly expressed in the homeostatic microglial states, and thus makes for a promising biomarker. In particular, P2Y12R PET tracers could complement translocator protein (TSPO) and P2X7 receptor tracers, which image microglial density or target the pro-inflammatory state, respectively. Unfortunately, current high-affinity P2Y12R ligands do not enter the brain because they are charged in vivo or because they are substrates for efflux transporters. Attempts to increase brain uptake by improving their physicochemical properties have not yet resulted in a successful P2Y12R PET tracer. This emphasizes the need for novel chemotypes. Herein, we applied a pharmacophore-based virtual screening strategy to a library of about three million compounds. As a result, we identified the imidazo[1,2-b]pyrazolone scaffold as a promising structural class to use as a starting point for developing P2Y12R ligands. After extensive hit expansion and structure-activity relationship studies, the two best ligands displayed excellent binding affinity for human P2Y12R (96: Ki = 9.61 ± 1.70 nM; 109: Ki = 3.10 ± 0.34 nM) and rat P2Y12R (96: Ki = 65.6 ± 25.9 nM; 109: Ki = 17.9 ± 12.8 nM) in a radioligand binding assay. Furthermore, imidazo[1,2-b]pyrazolone [18F]91 was successfully radiolabeled as a proof-of-concept in sufficient radiochemical yields. Future work will assess whether the more potent ligands can be radiolabeled and used to image the P2Y12R in the brain. Together, these results highlight the use of pharmacophore-based strategy in PET tracer development and provide a robust basis for further hit exploration.

item.title: Disentangling protein confinement from surface adsorption in hierarchical zirconium metal-organic frameworks
item.description: A persistent challenge in protein immobilization within metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) is distinguishing genuine internal confinement from surface adsorption and interparticle voids, which can mimic encapsulation despite fundamentally different spatial microenvironments. Incorporating mesochannels to produce hierarchical UiO-66-NH2 and MOF-808 nanoparticles, prepared by micelle templating, offers a strategy to overcome this ambiguity while preserving their intrinsic microporosity. Evidence from pore accessibility, pulsed field gradient NMR, and small-angle X-ray scattering is consistent with protein association within mesochannel environments. In the hierarchical hosts, loaded bovine serum albumin shows enhanced resilience to thermal stress. Together, these results are consistent with internal mesochannel confinement contributing to protein stabilization while preserving molecular accessibility in MOFs. Extending confinement to function, Candida antarctica lipase B immobilized in these hosts remains catalytically active at elevated temperature. In contrast to a commercial immobilized preparation, it retains a larger fraction of its activity in the first reuse cycles.

item.title: Multinuclear High-Field FlowNMR for Real-Time Monitoring and Analysis of Biocatalytic Reactions in Batch and Flow
item.description: Online high-field nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy in continuous or recirculating flow (FlowNMR) offers a powerful yet underutilised approach for monitoring biocatalytic reactions, particularly in challenging aqueous and low-concentration systems. Herein, we demonstrate the application of multinuclear high-resolution FlowNMR at 500 MHz for real-time analysis of both batch and continuous flow biotransformations. Across four case studies run at the typical low concentrations associated with biocatalysis including alcohol oxidation, nitroreductase-mediated reduction, a two-stage enzymatic cascade and a nucleoside phosphorylation, high-resolution spectra were obtained without interference from enzymes or reaction media. This technique enabled direct observation of key reaction intermediates, rapid optimisation of conditions and structure elucidation at sub-millimolar concentrations. Overall, this work demonstrates online high-field NMR as a versatile and information-rich tool for biocatalysis, providing real-time insight and significantly accelerating reaction development, with strong potential for integration into automated flow systems.

item.title: Foundation interatomic potentials learn the practical chemistry they were never taught
item.description: Chemists understand molecular reactivity through simplified concepts such as substituent effects, acidity, and aromaticity, which are compact descriptors of the potential energy surface and of the electronic structure that shapes it. Universal machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) are transforming applied computational chemistry by learning the same surface from atomic structures, energies, and forces, making atomistic simulations of complex systems practical. Like chemists, MLIPs build compact internal representations of that surface, yet these are usually treated as a means to faster, larger-scale molecular dynamics simulations. Here we show that they also contain directly recoverable chemical information: simple models applied to the invariant per-atom embeddings of pretrained universal MLIPs recover Hammett substituent constants, Brønsted and Lewis acidity, and ring aromaticity with Spearman ρ = 0.8–0.99. The same representations predict the yield of a four-component palladium-catalyzed cross-coupling at ρ = 0.96, matching models built from curated descriptors, while pinpointing the aryl halide as the reaction’s key substrate and ranking isoxazole additives by catalyst-poisoning strength. Universal MLIPs are therefore not only fast engines for energies and forces but also chemically meaningful representations of molecular reactivity, opening a route to extracting chemical insights directly from the learned potentials themselves.

item.title: Stepwise Condensation to Diversify Cyano-Substituted Vinylene-Linked COFs for Boosting H2O2 Photosynthesis
item.description: Driven by growing demand for structural diversification and practical application of vinylene-linked covalent organic frameworks (COFs), it is critical to develop sustainable routes to monomers with highly tunable connectivity and functionality. Herein, we report an efficient route to a new class of aromatic DCP derivatives (DCP = 2,6-dimethyl-3,5-dicyanopyridine) via Hantzsch-type condensation from low-cost commodity chemicals. Using arene-bridged DCP dimers (arene = phenyl, biphenyl, naphthalenyl) as tetratopic monomers, we constructed three new vinylene-linked COFs via Knoevenagel condensation with 4,4'-biphenyldicarbaldehyde. Thorough characterization reveals their long-range ordered structures and high porosity. Their semiconducting properties are finely tuned by varying the monomer arene bridges. In pure water, these COFs deliver excellent photocatalytic H2O2 production up to 7020 μmol g-1 h-1, outperforming the cyano-free counterpart. This phenomenon can be directly attributed to the abundant cyano substituents with strong dipolar and π-extended character in the as-prepared COFs. These cyano moieties enhance light harvesting and photogenerated charge utilization, and provide strong hydrogen-bonding interactions to stabilize the key *OOH intermediate, thereby facilitating oxygen reduction, as supported by theoretical investigations. This work provides an economical strategy to tailor vinylene-linked COF structures and functions for broader practical applications.

item.title: Shell-nested virtual spaces from atomic natural orbitals
item.description: Selecting a compact molecular virtual space requires deciding which radial and angular freedom can be removed while retaining a useful description of electron correlation. A correlated molecular density can guide this choice, but obtaining it requires a preliminary correlation calculation. Here we examine whether tabulated atomic natural orbitals (ANOs) can provide radial guidance within the previously introduced shell-nested framework. Complete multicenter overlaps select directions available in the molecular parent basis, while adaptation uses the restricted Hartree–Fock reference and earlier layers remain fixed. The resulting shell-nested virtual spaces, SNVS(ANO), improve the average energy recovery over density-guided shell spaces in the tested second-order Møller–Plesset (MP2) and coupled-cluster singles and doubles (CCSD) panels. ANO guidance narrows the mean raw-energy differences from equally sized MP2-based frozen natural orbital spaces, although the latter retain smaller parent truncation errors. The prescribed shell content also makes the successive additions of spatial flexibility explicit. These results show that correlated atomic radial functions can guide molecular virtual-space selection before a correlated molecular density is available. The molecular reference controls their adaptation, and the correction and extrapolation tests show that retention of finite-parent correlation must still be distinguished from accuracy against an independent explicitly correlated reference.

item.title: Ladderane as a Saturated Bioisostere of ortho-Benzene
item.description: Previously, we proposed a hypothesis that ladderanes could mimic ortho-benzene in bioactive compounds. In this work, we have proven this hypothesis experimentally. In particular, 2,3-disubstituted ladderanes were efficiently synthesized and extensively characterized. These cores were then incorporated into six bioactive compounds instead of the benzene ring. The corresponding patent-free ladderane derivatives of Thalidomide and Oxatomide showed improved physicochemical profiles and similar biological activities compared to those of the original drugs. These results confirm that ladderanes can act as saturated bioisosteres of ortho-benzenes.

item.title: Chemical Editing of DNA-Mediated Nanoparticle Superlattices through a CRISPR-inspired Strategy
item.description: Biological systems employ molecular machinery to organize matter into functional structures and dynamically modify their organization in response to external signals. Translating such capabilities into synthetic nanomaterials requires strategies to selectively modify the interactions that define their structure. DNAbased assembly exploits sequence-specific molecular recognition to organize nanoscale components into prescribed architectures, yet post-assembly modification of structural DNA bonds remains challenging. Here, we demonstrate that enzymatic reactions, such as DNA-backbone covalent scission using CRISPRmediated editing of DNA linkers, provide targeted chemical modification of assembled 3D nanomaterials. Guide RNAs (gRNAs) direct Cas9 and Cas12a nucleases to selectively cleave DNA duplexes linking nanoparticles within ordered superlattices. Fluorescence measurements, optical microscopy, and timeresolved small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) reveal how molecular bond cleavage propagates into domain erosion, fragmentation, and loss of long-range lattice order. We extend this strategy to superlattices assembled from DNA-origami frames, demonstrating programmable disassembly through chemical cleavage of interframe DNA linkages. Importantly, sequence-selective disassembly can be realized within mixed populations of DNA-origami lattices, where Cas9 selectively disrupts lattices containing the recognized linker sequence, while non-targeted lattices retain their structure within the same reaction environment. These results establish sequence-specific chemical modification of DNA bonds as a strategy for selectively transforming DNA-based nanomaterials. This approach extends DNA programmability beyond encoding the initial assembly to directing post-assembly transformations, providing a pathway toward nanomaterials whose organization can be selectively modified through guided enzymatic processes,

item.title: Isolable silyl- and germyl-thioketones dearomatize their own benzene rings at room temperature
item.description: Although dearomatization of benzene converts flat molecules into three-dimensional (3D) frameworks, the stability of the benzene ring makes this transformation difficult. Main-group compounds that achieve it are typically highly reactive low-valent species or contain weak multiple bonds and usually require elaborate design. Thioketones engage an adjacent aryl ring only with strongly electron-poor partners or fused arenes, and the products rearomatize. Whether a simple, isolable main-group functional group can dearomatize a non-fused benzene ring under mild conditions has remained unclear so far. Here, we introduce a substituent-based strategy that switches on this reactivity, i.e., thioketones bearing a σ-donating silyl or germyl group dearomatize their own benzene rings at room temperature without the need for metals, light, or redox reagents. Whereas conventional thioketones are inert toward alkenes under identical conditions, these compounds, including the first structurally characterized silyl-thioketone and the first isolable germyl-thioketones, undergo cascade cycloadditions with alkenes and alkynes to give air-stable 3D frameworks. Rather than strengthening frontier-orbital interactions, the group-14 substituent polarizes the C═S bond and renders bond formation highly asynchronous, thus markedly reducing the distortion required to disrupt the aromatic ring. These results establish main-group substitution as a design strategy for unlocking latent dearomative reactivity under mild conditions.

item.title: Ni/TiO2 Interfaces Enhance Benzaldehyde Selectivity in the Photocatalytic Dehydrogenation of Benzyl Alcohol
item.description: The selective conversion of alcohols to carbonyls (ketones and aldehydes) plays an important role in chemical manufacturing. Photocatalytic acceptorless dehydrogenation offers a light-driven alternative for producing value-added aldehydes and H2 under mild conditions and with easy separation and high molar efficiency. However, using semiconductor photocatalysts to achieve high selectivity and long-term stability under prolonged high-intensity illumination remains challenging. In this work, we developed CdS/TiO2/Ni photocatalysts by depositing TiO2 onto CdS nanoparticle panels via atomic layer deposition (ALD), followed by Ni cocatalyst photodeposition, for the acceptorless dehydrogenation of benzyl alcohol to benzaldehyde and H2. Diluting the benzyl alcohol concentration to a practical range of ~10 vol% (1 M) further increased benzaldehyde selectivity to ~95%. Ni photodeposition and zeta-potential measurements suggest that TiO2 coatings progressively modify Cd2+-associated surface sites through Ti3+/Ti4+ incorporation, altering adsorption kinetics and contributing to the reduced activity. This extends the photocatalyst’s lifespan from ~23 to 60 hours and increases cumulative benzaldehyde and H2 production. TiO2 thin-film coatings have emerged as a promising strategy to protect semiconductor photocatalysts while modifying surface active sites and reaction kinetics, and their stability-activity trade-off showing lower initial-stage activity beyond 15-cycle ALD will be discussed alongside proposed mechanisms. This work establishes a semiconductor/coating/cocatalyst design architecture that highlights the importance of engineering surface adsorption and active-site environments, alongside charge-separation strategies based on band-edge energetics and charge-carrier dynamics, to jointly optimize photocatalytic activity and product selectivity for targeted chemical synthesis.

item.title: Correcting the Liquid Densities of Universal Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials Using Local-Number-Density Repulsion
item.description: Universal machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) such as UMA, trained on reference data from meta-generalized gradient approximation or hybrid functionals that incorporate dispersion interactions, often overestimate molecular-liquid densities, thereby placing every property computed at constant pressure at the wrong state point. This study proposes a correction that adds to the MLIP a repulsive energy quadratic in the local number density of each atom, with two coefficients fitted only to the equations of state of water and ethanol; the forces and stresses follow analytically, so neither electronic-structure calculations nor retraining is required. For UMA, the correction reduces the density mean absolute error (MAE) of 22 liquids from 10.8% to 2.5%, lowering the error for every liquid and bringing 20 of them within ±5% of experiment, while improving the bulk modulus (MAE from 71.6% to 22.1%), heat of vaporization, and second hydration shell of water, none of which was calibrated.
