Its volumetric CO2 capture flux exceeds that of the best reported 18 flue-gas capture systems by more than 2.7-fold and that of current DAC technologies by 5.8-19 fold. For DAC at a capture capacity of 1 ton of CO2 per day, this perfrmance translates to a 20 ≈10-fold reduction in required contactor volume relative to conventional air-liquid contactors.

item.title: Neural quantum states for non-Markovian open quantum dynamics in bosonic environments
item.description: Condensed-phase quantum dynamics are strongly shaped by vibrational, solvent, and protein environments, yet their nonperturbative, non-Markovian description requires a rapidly growing high-dimensional representation as environmental complexity increases. Here, we extend neural quantum states (NQS) to the dissipaton-embedded quantum master equation (DQME) for bosonic environments using a complex-valued restricted Boltzmann machine adapted to nonbinary bosonic occupations. An explicit filtering scheme further concentrates the neural representation on dynamically relevant dissipaton configurations. The resulting NQS-DQME approach reproduces representative quantum dissipative dynamics while effectively compressing the reduced density tensor (RDT). For an anharmonic model of condensed-phase hydrogen transfer, the method also reproduces weak-coupling tunneling dynamics. At stronger system-bath coupling, however, errors become localized in a small subset of RDT elements, showing that a small global variational residual does not necessarily ensure accurate chemically relevant observables. This limitation identifies observable-level error control as a key challenge for reliable long-time NQS propagation.

item.title: Noise Ceilings for Molecular Potency Benchmarks: Measuring Label Noise from Independent ChEMBL Documents
item.description: The same compound measured against the same target in different laboratories often receives different potency values, which limits how well any model can be scored against such labels. For 17 potency tasks (target × Ki or IC50) from ChEMBL 37, we estimate this limit per task from 3,292 molecules reported in at least two source documents and express model scores as a fraction of ceiling f (0: predicting the training mean; 1: reaching the estimated noise floor). The floors range from 0.31 to 0.79 pChEMBL units, but for some tasks the replicates come from a few document pairs, and a bootstrap over document pairs then gives intervals several times wider than one over molecules. After removing molecules found in MoleculeNet and TDC, we benchmark ECFP-based gradient boosting, random forest and MLP models and frozen ChemBERTa-77M and MoLFormer-XL embeddings with a boosted-tree head under random, scaffold and temporal splits. ECFP with a random forest reaches a mean f of 0.90, 0.73 and 0.36 on the three splits (random: median 0.82, range 0.80–1.03 over the floor’s uncertainty). The frozen embeddings reach 0.69/0.66, 0.55/0.54 and 0.25/0.25 (ChemBERTa/MoLFormer) and are below ECFP with gradient boosting on every split (Wilcoxon over tasks, Holm-adjusted p < 0.05); on five tasks, a D-MPNN and a fine-tuned ChemBERTa do not close the gap on random and scaffold splits. On five task–split combinations ECFP models score below the estimated floor (f > 1), which shows that the floor is uncertain for these tasks; we discuss mis-estimation and learnable document-level offsets as explanations. We report single-test-set minimum detectable effects and a reporting protocol, and release code and data.

item.title: Mobilis: an open-source toolkit for charge transport in organic semiconductors, from crystal structures to temperaturedependent mobilities with dynamic disorder and active learning
item.description: Computing a charge mobility for an organic semiconductor involves a chain of steps: monomer site energies, intermolecular couplings, the thermal fluctuation of those couplings, and a transport model whose validity depends on the ratio of coupling to reorganization energy. These steps are usually carried out with separate scripts and different quantum-chemistry codes, which makes results hard to reproduce and models hard to compare. Mobilis is an open-source Python package (GPL-3.0) with a graphical interface and a command-line interface that runs the whole chain from a CIF file or an MD morphology. It prepares and reads Gaussian and ADF calculations (and xtb from the command line), and contains its own extended-Hückel and ZINDO couplings, a polarizable site-energy model, Marcus–Jortner hopping with kinetic Monte Carlo, and transient localization theory. For dynamic disorder it builds coupling surfaces over the six rigidbody intermolecular coordinates and samples them by full-crystal rigid-body molecular dynamics. A Gaussian-process active-learning loop chooses the DFT dimer calculations needed for these surfaces and stops when the posterior uncertainty of the coupling fluctuation σV falls below a target. For pentacene, 24–40 DFT dimers per pair reproduce σV within 4%, against 273 points for a quadratic fit. Chiral molecules in centrosymmetric crystals, such as mer-Alq3 and Ir(III) emitters, are treated by mirror-image fragments. The code is tested by 34 automated test scripts, including an exact-solution check of the kinetic Monte Carlo, and is archived on Zenodo (doi:10.5281/zenodo.23593488).

item.title: Semisyntheses of Aspercyclicins A and B via Isobenzofuran Cycloaddition
item.description: The recently isolated aspercyclicins A and B from Aspergillus sp. LI2020F001 represent a chimeric scaffold derived from crosstalk of two biosynthetic pathways. These natural products display cytotoxicity against cancer cell lines and potently activate immunogenic cell death (ICD). Herein, we report methodology development for biomimetic [4+2] cycloadditions involving an in situ generated isobenzofuran (IBF) leading to the semisyntheses of aspercyclicins A and B from the fungal-derived natural product (+)-geodin.

item.title: Methodological Optimization of ATR-IR Spectroelectrochemistry for Powdered and Poorly Conductive Electrocatalysts
item.description: In-situ infrared spectroscopy combined with electrochemistry has become a key tool for studying the processes that govern the activity of electrocatalysts under operating conditions. However, its application has been limited almost exclusively to model electrodes, which are either electronically conductive or specifically designed to maximise the ATR optical signal, thereby limiting its use for a family of emerging heterogenous catalysts typically available in powder form and exhibiting poor electrical conductivity. Extending ATR-IR spectroelectrochemistry to this type of catalyst requires simultaneously reconciling optical, adhesion and electrochemical requirements which, until now, have rarely been addressed systematically. Rather than focusing on the elucidation of electrocatalyst mechanisms, this paper presents a structured and transferable methodology for optimising ATR-IR spectroelectrochemical measurements on emerging classes of electrocatalyst. Three groups of interrelated parameters that mostly affect the feasibility of the technique, namely spectroscopic, interfacial and electrochemical parameters, are discussed proposing a step-by-step workflow that enables their methodological standardization and balance. The proposed workflow is validated by applying this methodology to three different materials (Ni(OH)2, ZnO and Zn-Al LDH) showing distinct spectroscopic, electrochemical and interfacial properties. The results demonstrate that, following appropriate optimisation, ATR spectroelectrochemistry can be extended to more challenging powdered catalyst layers, providing a practical and generalisable guide for future robust mechanistic investigations of this broad family of materials and contributing to the rational understanding and development of new electrocatalysts for reactions of energy and chemical interest.

item.title: Programming Chemoselectivity in Aerobic Oxidation through Zr-MOF/Quinone Multicatalysis for Benzazole Synthesis
item.description: Selectivity control in aerobic oxidation reactions containing several oxidizable functional groups remains challenging. Herein, we show that the chemoselectivity of a Zr-MOF/quinone multicatalytic platform can be controlled through modulation of the organic redox co-catalyst. In contrast to previously reported Zr-MOF-808/(hydro)quinone combinations that promote direct heteroatom oxidation in anilines or thiols to yield the corresponding azoxy or disulfide compounds, Zr-MOF-808/1,8-dichloroanthraquinone unlocks a different reaction pathway to selectively oxidize primary alcohols in the presence of aromatic diamines and aminothiophenols. This pathway enables the one-pot synthesis of 2-substituted benzimidazoles and benzothiazoles under atmospheric air. Mechanistic experiments and post-reaction catalyst characterization support coupled catalytic cycles in which Lewis-acidic Zr sites in the MOF facilitate quinone-mediated alcohol oxidation, while the redox-active MOF/semiquinone interface regenerates the catalytic cycle using atmospheric oxygen as the terminal oxidant. This method furnishes a highly practical and sustainable synthesis of 31 benzimidazoles and benzothiazoles including commercially relevant products such as thiabendazole and fuberidazole, permitting recovery and reuse of both catalytic components.

item.title: Footprint-aware Microkinetics Reveal Spatial Correlations with Catalytic Consequences
item.description: Metal catalysis often involves bulky molecules that cover catalyst surface areas beyond a single exposed metal atom. Common multi-site models account for adsorbate size with simple mean-field correction factors, but neglect how multi-site adsorbates become spatially correlated to avoid overlapping. Here, we combine prior theoretical constructions—the reduction of the Master equation in the fast-diffusion limit and the Widom insertion approach—to develop a footprint-aware microkinetic framework where adsorbates interact through hard exclusion. We use Monte Carlo simulations to construct surrogate models of vacant site clusters and neighboring reactant pairs needed for elementary reaction steps, which introduce missing footprint effects into conventional kinetic models. These models retain explicit kinetic and thermodynamic parameters, support standard mechanistic analyses, and can be reused across temperatures and reaction conditions without repeated configurational sampling. We illustrate the framework using unimolecular and bimolecular reactions of an adsorbate with a seven-site footprint, resembling benzene and phenol. Footprint-induced correlations have two effects relative to mean-field treatments: they (i) enrich the sites surrounding multi-site adsorbates with single-site co-adsorbates or vacancies, and (ii) aggregate empty sites into clusters that accommodate additional multi-site adsorbates. These correlations alter absolute rates, reactant pressure trends, step reversibilities, and degrees of rate control. The correlation effects are most pronounced for bimolecular reactions when surfaces are crowded by multi-site adsorbates and adsorption events at single sites or site pairs are kinetically relevant. For one bimolecular reaction, the mean-field approximation fits footprint-aware rates and elementary-step reversibility across a given range of pressures for a single reactant, but only after reducing the apparent footprint from seven to 3.3 sites and weakening the adsorption free energy by 12 RT. The approximation furthermore predicts different coreactant pressure dependences. Consequently, quantitative model agreement with kinetic trends can conceal physically inaccurate parameters and mechanistic interpretations when accounting for adsorbate size, while neglecting spatial correlations.

item.title: Rapid One-Step Synthesis of Sodium-Ion Battery Cathodes from Desalination Waste: A Sustainable Approach to High-Performance Energy Storage
item.description: Desalination brine, a hypersaline byproduct of water treatment processes, represents an underutilized sodium feedstock with significant potential for battery material production. In this work, we report a streamlined rapid one-step synthesis (ROSS) method for Na3V2(PO4)3 (NVP), a highperformance sodium-ion battery cathode material with demonstrated electrochemical comparability with lithium-based alternatives, directly from desalination brine. Sequential filtration and chemical precipitation were used to selectively isolate sodium ions from brine, effectively removing divalent cations (Ca2+, Mg2+), heavy metal impurities and organic contaminants. The purified sodiumion solution was subsequently used to prepare a sodium-vanadium-oxalate precursor, from which phase-pure NVP crystals with carbon coating were obtained via a single-step combustion reaction. Notably, the entire crystallization process was completed within 45 minutes using an open crucible setup under ambient atmosphere, representing a significant reduction in both processing time and operational complexity compared to conventional NVP synthesis routes, which typically require 2–4 hours under inert gas conditions. Our method offers a dual environmental benefit: mitigating the ecological impact of brine discharge while supplying a low-cost, sustainable sodium source for the growing sodium-ion battery industry.

item.title: Untargeted Lipidomics Reveals Dynamic Changes to the HEK 293T Lipidome During Lentiviral Vector Production Over 72 Hours
item.description: Lentiviral vectors (LV) are biotechnology tools descending from human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) that may be used in cell and gene therapies. HIV transduction efficiency has been shown to be negatively affected when the lipid composition of its envelope is altered, suggesting that targeted lipid envelope composition engineering may serve as a tool to modulate transduction. To investigate this possibility, an untargeted lipidomics experiment was conducted on HEK 293T packaging cells producing LV at three time points: 24, 48 and 72 h. 401 lipids from 23 classes were identified and significant changes to the HEK 293T lipidome from LV production were recorded at each time point. Triacylglycerol (TG) and phosphatidylcholine (PC) species were the most affected lipid classes throughout the time course. Large increases in the abundance of TG species were observed with significant depletion of many PC species, suggesting lipid droplet formation occurs during LV production. Analysis of the fatty acyl chain profiles revealed that LV production significantly increased the average chain length after 24 and 48 h while the double bond index did not change in a statistically significant manner across all time points compared to control cells, possibly serving as a means to maintain homeostasis while large amounts of shorter acyl chains were used for LV envelope formation. 9 of 12 acyl chains had significant trends with increased LV production time, serving as targets for media supplementation or for metabolic pathway manipulation to increase LV titer. Future directions will investigate the effects of media supplementation with phospholipid mixtures on the dynamics of TG species over time with LV production.

item.title: Molecular Autocatalysis through Interfacial Recruitment of Catalytic Functional Groups
item.description: Autocatalysis enables nonlinear reactivity, self-amplification, and emergent chemical behavior. At the soft interfaces of emulsions and vesicles, autocatalysis has been linked to dynamic behavior such as growth, propagation, and oscillations. Most reported interfacial autocatalytic systems rely on assembly-driven physical effects such as reactant colocalization rather than well-defined catalytic interactions. Whether catalytic function can be molecularly encoded within assemblies, independent of assembly formation itself, remains unresolved. Here we demonstrate molecular autocatalysis through interfacial recruitment of catalytic functional groups. As product accumulates, catalytic groups are concentrated at the interface, creating a positive feedback loop that accelerates further synthesis. The molecular identity of the product, rather than assembly formation, controls autocatalytic behavior. We further show the generality of this mechanism across two distinct reaction classes, oxime condensation and thiol-Michael addition. Autocatalytic lipids self-assemble into growing vesicles, coupling molecular feedback to compartment propagation and establishing a general chemical strategy for self-amplifying soft matter systems.

item.title: Fragment-Grounded Neural Simulation of Electron Ionization Mass Spectra at Library Scale
item.description: Electron ionization mass spectrometry (EI-MS) is a sensitive analytical technique, yet compound identification conventionally relies on reference libraries that contain spectra for at most about one million compounds, which is a small subset of chemical space. In silico prediction of EI-MS spectra can extend these libraries, but existing data-driven models generalize poorly beyond their training distribution, and physics-based simulations are too costly for library-scale use. Here, we present a fragment-grounded neural workflow that predicts an EI-MS spectrum by exhaustively enumerating the fragmentation graph of a molecule and then assigning intensities to the resulting substructures with a model trained on experimental spectra. By relating every predicted peak back to a candidate substructure, our model generalizes more reliably to unseen scaffolds and out-of-distribution chemistry than prior fingerprint- and black-box transformer-based predictors. On a scaffold split, it identifies the correct structure among up to fifty same-formula isomers in 43.0% of cases, compared to 32.5% for the strongest baseline. Further, it matches the accuracy of quantum-chemical simulation while being roughly seven orders of magnitude faster. To test the model's capabilities under a harder, formula-agnostic setting, we further evaluate retrieval against a library of 87.3 million compounds from PubChem. There, our model achieves a top-1 accuracy of 3.3%, compared to 1.1% for the strongest baseline, and a peak-mass-window filter further raises its top-1 accuracy to 5.3%. The predicted spectra for 87.3 million compounds serve as an augmented reference library to facilitate database-dependent structure elucidation.

item.title: Sustainable Surface Metallurgy for Public Health: A Review of Barrier Degradation, Structural Heterogeneity, and Aluminum Leaching Dynamics in Low-Income Country Cookware
item.description: Aluminum (Al) consumer cookware remains a cornerstone of global food preparation due to its exceptional thermal efficiency and low cost. However, in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), the widespread reliance on low-purity, informally recycled artisanal alloys creates severe public health risks due to heavy metal migration into dietary pathways. This review explicitly links materials engineering for sustainable development with global safety frameworks by evaluating surface modification technologies designed to mitigate aluminum ion leaching under aggressive thermal and chemical cooking conditions. This review systematically synthesizes the thermodynamic, kinetic, and mechanical performance of three dominant protective systems: electrochemical anodization, sol-gel quasi-ceramic matrices, and fluoropolymer barriers. The chemical stability of these systems is analyzed using mass transport models, chelation-assisted coordination mechanics, and the Arrhenius activation energy framework. Furthermore, a sequential technical characterization workflow is established—linking Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM-EDX), X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS), and Inductively Coupled Plasma Mass Spectrometry (ICP-MS)—to evaluate barrier performance against the strict specific migration limits (SML) enforced by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) and the United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA). While hard anodization and ceramic coatings offer excellent thermal stability, their long-term barrier performance is often compromised by interfacial shear stresses driven by mismatched coefficients of thermal expansion (CTE) and mechanical wear. This issue is particularly severe in informal metallurgical sectors. Artisanal castings feature high structural porosity and iron/copper micro-impurities that create localized galvanic micro-cells (Δ E > 1.0 V), accelerating the breakdown of surface oxide barriers and leading to heavy metal migration that routinely exceeds international safety standards by factors of 10 to 50. Critical commercial research gaps are identified, specifically the development of cost-effective, bio-based non-stick barriers (e.g., cross-linked green nanocomposites) and the implementation of decentralized circular economy scrap-sorting upgrades. Resolving these material vulnerabilities is essential for advancing UN Sustainable Development Goals related to good health and well-being (SDG 3), clean manufacturing (SDG 9), and responsible consumption and production (SDG 12). This work provides a clear roadmap for scalable, non-hazardous cookware manufacturing tailored for vulnerable populations.

item.title: Elucidating thermodynamic infeasibility of the (de)-lithiation process in 5V-class LiNi0.5Ge1.5O4 solid electrolyte
item.description: LiNi0.5Ge1.5O4 (LNGO), a Ge-substituted analogue of high-voltage cobalt-free LiNi0.5Mn1.5O4 (LNMO) spinel cathode, has previously been reported to show electrochemical inertness up to 5V vs. Li+/Li. However, thermodynamic and electronic origins of this inert behaviour have remained unexplored. Herein, we investigated the redox mechanism and thermodynamic driving force governing the (de)intercalation behaviour of LNGO using first-principles density functional theory (DFT+U) and verified using experimental findings. Convex hull analysis over the compositional range (0<x<2 in LixNi0.5Ge1.5O4) reveals absence of stable or metastable intermediate phases, supporting electrochemical inert behaviour. This was further reinforced by substantial evolution of structural symmetry, lattice parameters, and electronic band gaps during the process of (de)lithiation, resulting in a high-voltage stability up to 5 V vs. Li+/Li. Moreover, AIMD and CI-NEB calculations predicted Li-ion migration via vacant octahedral sites with a moderately high activation barrier of 0.537 eV. Experimental techniques such as linear sweep voltammetry, electrochemical impedance analysis and chronoamperometry were used to confirm DFT findings. These findings suggests that LNGO can be used as a possible solid electrolyte candidate in high energy density battery applications.

item.title: Revisiting Percolation and Molecular Diffusion in Disordered Pore Networks
item.description: The relationship between pore network structure and molecular diffusion in disordered nanoporous materials remains unclear. Here, we revisit two methodological choices that may contribute to inconsistent structure–diffusion relationships in the literature: percolation characterization and inclusion of non-percolating pores in diffusivity calculations. Our rigorous benchmarks show consistent results from Zeo++ and Mofography but reveal biased characterization from PoreBlazer due to limitations in its algorithm. Molecular dynamics simulations further consolidate that initializing adsorbates in percolating pore networks is essential for reliable and robust calculations of molecular self-diffusivity. With these issues addressed, we re-examine structure–diffusion relationships for methane across four amorphous material classes. Symbolic regression identifies the percolating backbone fraction as a key, yet largely overlooked, topology-related descriptor that captures a common diffusion trend across classes. Further analysis supports the added predictive value of this new descriptor beyond conventional geometric descriptors in machine learning tasks. Our work provides a consistent methodological foundation and a complementary descriptor for diffusion prediction in disordered nanoporous materials.

item.title: An Enzyme-DNA Nanostructure with Enhanced Catalysis Accelerates MRSA Wound Healing
item.description: Antibiotic-resistant wound infections are a growing clinical challenge, as bacteria evade singletarget antimicrobials and persist within protective biofilms. Antimicrobial enzymes offer a promising alternative through their catalytic generation of bactericidal species, but their therapeutic utility is limited by instability in protease-rich wound environments. Here, we demonstrate that densely grafting short DNA strands onto lactoperoxidase (LPO), an innate immune enzyme, creates an enzyme-DNA nanostructure (Nano-Lac) with enhanced proteolytic stability and catalytic activity. Whereas polymer conjugation typically compromises enzyme activity, DNA functionalization increased LPO’s catalytic turnover by >10-fold. Mechanistic studies revealed conformational changes consistent with increased active-site accessibility and reduced accumulation of an inactive oxidized intermediate under excess H2O2. These enhancements translated into broad-spectrum activity against multidrug-resistant Escherichia coli (E. coli) and methicillinresistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). Nano-Lac suppressed growth, disrupted biofilms, and compromised membrane integrity, outperforming vancomycin in vitro. In a murine MRSA wound model, daily topical Nano-Lac reduced bacterial burden ~2-fold and accelerated wound closure versus native LPO and vancomycin, without histopathological signs of toxicity. Extending beyond LPO, DNA functionalization also enhanced peroxidase activity across structurally distinct heme proteins, including myoglobin, hemoglobin, and cytochrome c. These findings establish DNA grafting as a general strategy to enhance heme-protein stability, catalysis, and therapeutic function.

item.title: Anisotropic Electrical Conductivity in Close-Packed Two-Dimensional Polyaramids
item.description: Polyaramids such as Kevlar® are renowned for their high mechanical strength and chemical resistance; however, their non-conjugated backbones render them electrically insulating. Orbital alignment can allow close-packed stacked molecules to exhibit long range conduction, opening the possibility that insulating nanomaterials may form conducting arrangements. Herein, we report two-dimensional (2D) polyaramids with tailored end-groups that promote tighter molecular packing as their size decreases. Terminal groups with the size of a single methyl result in aligned films that exhibit highly anisotropic electrical conductivity up to 1.39 × 10–4 S m–1, comparable to or exceeding many undoped conjugated polymers. Charge transport occurs orthogonally across aligned, stacked polymer platelets while the in-plane direction remains insulating. The anisotropy reverses the behavior typically observed in-plane conduction of stacked 2D nanomaterials. The resulting films are photoconductive under 405 nm illumination with an external quantum efficiency of 0.62%. The mechanical and chemical stability of such conductive 2D polyaramids enables the first single-component, acid-stable polymer electrodes based on non-conjugated frameworks, capable of operating in harsh environments while exhibiting perfectly invariant cyclic capacitance for over 10,000 cycles at pH 2. The stability is enabled in part by the impermeability of such films to moisture and oxygen, underscored by their ability to suppress perovskite degradation with a 150 nm coating. Together, these findings underscore a newly realized mode of electrical conduction in close-packed 2D polymers, enabling ultra-lightweight and chemically stable electrodes for energy storage and sustainability applications.

item.title: Behaviour of TMT labelled peptides in solid phase extraction, liquid chromatography, electrospray ionisation, and data-dependent acquisition
item.description: In bottom-up proteomics, quantification with isobaric labelling involves derivatising peptides with reagents that are isobaric when intact but upon fragmentation produce reporter ions of different masses. Peptides from different samples are labelled with different reagent isotopomers, and the reporter ion intensities serve as a readout for peptide abundance in different samples, enabling sample multiplexing. Increased chromatographic retention of labelled peptides has been described and considered in models predicting peptide retention. However, how isobaric labelling affects peptide behaviour in other steps of the analytical workflow remains scarcely studied. In this work, we applied isobaric tandem mass tag (TMT) labelling on synthetic peptides to study how TMT labelling affects the peptides’ retention and yield in solid phase extraction, retention in liquid chromatography, and signal intensity. In addition, we monitored how closely reporter ion intensity reflects precursor ion intensity across chromatographic peaks. In solid phase extraction, TMT labelling caused a slight increase in retention without being detrimental to yield. In liquid chromatography, our results confirm those of earlier publications, identifying a retention increase, the magnitude of which is correlated with peptide hydrophilicity. We detected a near-consistent decrease of signal intensity in TMT-labelled peptides that may imply decreased ionisation efficiency but is likely mitigated by increased analyte amount that comes with multiplexing. Finally, we observed that although reporter-to-precursor ion ratios are mostly stable, for some peptides they vary enough to significantly affect quantification. Our results show that while TMT labelling affects peptide behaviour in analytics, changes to the analytical workflow are mostly not required.Graphical abstractGraphical abstractGraphical abstractGraphical abstract

item.title: Consistency Testing of an Integrated SWRO–Brine Valorization Architecture: Alkalinity as the Binding Constraint
item.description: Integrated seawater reverse osmosis (SWRO) with brine valorization is widely proposed as a route to lower energy and near-zero liquid discharge, but such architectures are rarely tested against the physical bounds their stages must obey. Here a consistency-testing framework is applied to an architecture combining subsurface intake, isobaric energy recovery, membrane brine concentration, selective Ca/Mg precipitation and mechanical-vapor-compression crystallization. Each subsystem is checked against a thermodynamic or stoichiometric constraint rather than an assumed value. The concentrator duty commonly assumed in this class of study, 0.5–1.0 kWh m−3 of brine, lies at or below the least work of separation for that feed, 0.94 kWh m−3. A bounded estimate from that minimum and a 25–55% second-law efficiency gives 1.7–3.8 kWh m−3, raising the modeled total specific energy consumption to a median of 13.1 kWh m−3. Magnesium recovery is limited by alkalinity rather than by magnesium. The base required carries 10.0 kg CO2 per cubic meter of permeate in embodied carbon, roughly double the plant's grid emissions, or 27 kWh m−3 if generated electrochemically. Lime dosing releases 5.3 times more calcium than the carbonate step removes, so the train does not close. Costing those reagents explicitly is decisive: at $1.70 m−3 they exceed the $1.25 m−3 mineral credit, and Monte Carlo propagation (300,000 samples) gives a net levelized cost of $2.20 m−3 against $0.76 m−3 for conventional SWRO. Closing the calcium balance costs $0.44 m−3; above $0.069 kWh−1 no on-site base can close the loop, because the reversible limit of water dissociation binds.

item.title: Disrupting Surface Oxo Availability Suppresses Ru Dissolution in RuO2 Electrocatalysts
item.description: Ru loss from RuO2 in acidic oxygen evolution requires availability of surface oxo (*O) for eruption of surface Ru to form adsorbed *RuO4. Screening 20 dopants on *O-covered RuO2(110) (DFT) gave a trend linking *RuO4 formation to dopant-dependent *O activity. Durability testing (CP, ICP-MS) followed this trend for Mo- and Ta-RuO2. Zn- and Hf-RuO2 retained more Ru than predicted; in situ near-ambient pressure XPS and online ICP-MS reveal that the two do so by different means. Zn inhibits Ru overoxidation while Hf welcomes it, yet both inhibit Ru eruption. Surface-modulated models in which Zn dissolution leaves a cation vacancy and Hf bears a surface *OH both exhibit enhanced Ru retention (DFT): cation vacancies electronically reduce neighboring Ru and lack *O, whereas Hf’s *OH permits Ru overoxidation but inhibits its eruption. Both catalysts retain high activity (LSV) through a Ru-centered oxygen evolution pathway (GC-DFT). These findings reveal how dopants can enhance Ru retention by disrupting *O participation, regardless of Ru oxidation state, all while maintaining high oxygen evolution activity.

item.title: Dynamic Disproportionation Shapes Ga Sites in Silica-Supported Propane Dehydrogenation Catalysts
item.description: Ga is a key component of commercial propane dehydrogenation (PDH) catalysts. The regeneration of those catalysts involves oxidation and reduction cycles, the latter typically under H2 at about 550–650 °C. However, the structural evolution of Ga3+ sites under those strongly reducing conditions is underexplored. Here, we monitored the transformations of Ga3+ sites dispersed on a SiO2 support under H2 at 650 °C. The results show that this treatment generates metastable ºSiOGa1+ sites that disproportionate to Ga0 and Ga3+ sites. The formed Ga0 species react with surface silanols, regenerating ºSiOGa1+ sites, and with water formed during the reduction of Ga3+ to Ga1+, ultimately yielding large crystalline particles of k-Ga2O3. In addition, an overall loss of Ga from the catalyst is observed and attributed to the formation of Ga0 and volatile Ga2O. The Lewis acidity of dispersed Ga3+ decreases when it interacts with weakly Lewis-basic ºSiOGa1+ motifs. All of these processes associated with ºSiOGa1+ sites decrease the number of dispersed Ga3+ sites and are therefore detrimental for PDH activity, except that dispersed Ga3+ sites formed from disproportionation of ºSiOGa1+ sites likely have increased strain, beneficial for PDH activity. While H2 treatment alone has a negative impact on the catalyst’s PDH activity and propene selectivity, an oxidative air treatment of the reduced catalyst terminates disproportionation dynamics by oxidizing Ga0 and increases the Ga-based activity relative to both the reduced and fresh catalysts. These findings suggest that the disproportionation of Ga1+ species under an H2 atmosphere appreciably affects gallium speciation, loading, and catalytic performance.

item.title: How thermostats change the thermodynamic, structural and dynamic properties of a Lennard-Jones liquid
item.description: Almost every molecular dynamics simulation is coupled to a thermostat, and every thermostat modifies the equations of motion whose solutions are then interpreted as the physics of the system. The algorithms are well established and their qualitative artefacts are well known, yet a quantitative comparison of the commonly used schemes under one protocol, with the statistical resolution needed to detect their effects, is rarely reported, presumably because such effects are small compared with the run-to-run scatter of a typical simulation. Such a comparison, however, is of practical importance, since it determines which observables a given thermostat can be trusted with. In this work, we compare six temperature-control schemes (windowed velocity rescaling, Berendsen, Nosé–Hoover chains, Langevin, the dissipative-particle-dynamics pair thermostat and canonical sampling through velocity rescaling) at up to four coupling strengths each against an energy-matched microcanonical reference, for the truncated-and-shifted Lennard-Jones liquid, with five independent realizations per case and with finite-size and timestep controls. We find that thermodynamic means and pair structure are the same for all schemes once the mean temperature is matched, whereas the fluctuations differ and the differences propagate into derived quantities such as the heat capacity. For transport, the decisive variable is whether the thermostat acts globally or locally, not how strongly it is coupled: the global schemes leave the self-diffusion coefficient and the viscosity equivalent to those of the microcanonical reference over the whole coupling range, whereas the local stochastic schemes damp diffusion once their friction approaches the intrinsic friction of the liquid. In particular, we show that the Langevin bias at five state points is reproduced to within 16%, with no fitted parameter, by a resistance-addition interpolation whose only input is the cage factor of overdamped Brownian dynamics, and that, once the periodic-box correction is carried over to the screened hydrodynamics of a Langevin liquid, the bath is predicted to remove in the thermodynamic limit a hydrodynamic contribution to diffusion that a finite box conceals. Our results also rationalize two implementation effects in LAMMPS, the kinetic-energy fluctuation deficit of strongly coupled Langevin dynamics and the failure of the stress-autocorrelation viscosity for a strongly coupled pair thermostat, which could otherwise be mistaken for physics. The comparison condenses into simple rules for the choice of a thermostat and its coupling time.

item.title: Resistance without a detectable bindingenergy penalty: distinct dynamic defects of gatekeeper and molecular-brake mutations in FGFR1–erdafitinib recognition
item.description: The backbone Cα–Cα distance widely used to report kinase molecular-brake status gives a false negative under a clinically relevant FGFR1 resistance mutation: the brake's side-chain contact is destabilized in every replicate, yet the criterion reports it intact. Acquired FGFR1 kinase-domain mutations limit the clinical durability of erdafitinib, the first approved pan-FGFR inhibitor; loss of binding affinity is the assumed mechanism. We tested two questions in a single design: nine all-atom MD trajectories of the erdafitinib-bound kinase domain (wild type, V561M and molecular-brake mutant N546K; three replicates each; 4.491 μs). First, what a fully replicated comparison can resolve: neither MM/GBSA nor MM/PBSA detected a mutation-associated change in binding free energy; the observed mutant-versus-WT ΔΔG values lie below the detection limit of the present replicate set and within the intrinsic uncertainty of the end-point methods (GB ANOVA p = 0.27; PB p = 0.054). A large, E3810-like penalty (≈5 kcal·mol-1) is excluded. Second, the brake itself—N546K destabilizes the persistent engaged state of the residue-546–Glu562 contact: occupancy falls to 16–55% across replicates, entirely below the 95–100% of WT and V561M, at unchanged Cα–Cα geometry, dwell times fall from tens of nanoseconds to sub-nanosecond flickers, and broken periods reach 19 ns. V561M leaves the brake contact intact and instead loosens the gatekeeper-flanking hydrophobic network (Leu484/Val492/Lys514), dispersing its conformational ensemble across replicates. Side-chain proximity occupancy thus emerges as an operational order parameter for the molecular brake; the kinetic corollary, altered rates at unchanged affinity, is testable by SPR/BLI and unbinding calculations.

item.title: Orochi: A Physics-Grounded Python Package for Pair Distribution Function Analysis of Crystalline and Low-Dimensional Materials
item.description: Atomic pair distribution function (PDF) analysis from X-ray total scattering is a powerful methodology for determining atomic structure and arrangements across crystalline, disordered, nanostructured, and low-dimensional materials on both laboratory and synchrotron instruments. Fundamentally, PDF analysis relies on two core pillars—PDF data reduction from one-dimensional (1D) total scattering profiles and real-space structural modeling—often accompanied in rapid-acquisition experiments by upstream two-dimensional (2D) detector image processing. However, conventional workflows remain fragmented across disconnected software tools, forcing researchers to manually combine multiple programs and preventing the simultaneous optimization of measurement reduction parameters and crystal structure parameters that is standard in X-ray Rietveld refinement. Furthermore, mainstream PDF modeling engines rely on legacy physical approximations: they enforce three-dimensional (3D) periodic boundary conditions (requiring artificial vacuum supercells for 2D nanosheets), treat atomic scattering factors as angle-independent constants (causing peak distortions in compounds with large atomic number contrast), and approximate number density baselines using macroscopic bulk volume assumptions. Here, the open-source, pure-Python architecture of Orochi (version 4.0) is presented, implementing physical calculations from scratch in Python (accelerated via Numba) to unify total scattering data reduction, symmetry-aware crystallographic modeling, and real-space PDF simulation alongside a dedicated high-Q 2D detector processing module within a self-contained Python environment. Originally developed for laboratory total scattering studies of pharmaceutical glasses and deployed as compiled executable (β-version) tools at SPring-8 beamlines, Orochi has been completely redesigned around an externalized parameter management core (orochi.base) in which parameters are stored in standardized Python dictionaries and accessed via hierarchical string addresses. By bringing parameters outside the calculation engines rather than locking them inside built-in optimizers, this architecture allows multiple module instances across data reduction and structural modeling to be optimized simultaneously by modern optimization algorithms, machine learning libraries, and autonomous AI agents. For structural simulation, intra-cell atomic pair vectors are decoupled from lattice translation vectors to natively support arbitrary periodic boundary conditions across 3D crystals, 2D nanosheets, 1D nanowires, and 0D clusters. The simulation engine incorporates the full scattering vector (Q) dependence of atomic form factors, enabling accurate modeling of heavy/light-element oxides and permitting direct instrumental calibration using standard CeO2 powder rather than monoatomic nickel substitutes. Furthermore, a sinc-convolution density formulation is established to accurately reproduce baseline ripples arising from finite Qmin cutoffs in nanostructured systems. Complete mathematical formulations for all reduction and simulation algorithms are consolidated to establish a rigorous foundation for automated crystallographic analysis.

item.title: Development of oligo-thioester precursors for native chemical ligation of oligo-protein conjugates.
item.description: Protein-oligo conjugates have emerged as a promising therapeutic modality that unites the target-specificity and favorable pharmacokinetics of a protein carrier with the potency of an oligonucleotide payload. One challenge in the development of these biologics is that conjugation strategies often yield heterogeneous, high drug-to-antibody ratio (DAR) products or require non-canonical amino acids and multi-step handling. Native chemical ligation (NCL) is a promising tool for protein-oligo conjugation, as the reaction is single-step and regiospecific to N-terminal cysteines, which can be genetically installed into proteins in a facile manner. However, methods for generating the required oligo-thioesters remain a technical challenge, especially when complex linker groups are desired. Here, we report an efficient protocol to generate four oligo linker-payloads (LPs) incorporating an anti-sense oligonucleotide targeting the MALAT1 gene, bis(2-sulfanylethyl)amine (NSS)- or thioacid-based thioester precursors, and diverse intervening linkers. The LPs were successfully ligated to an affibody and the crystallizable fragment (Fc) of an antibody, key protein carriers for protein-oligo therapeutics. The operationally simple, bespoke nature of this workflow enables the diversification of oligo payloads and linkers required for broad applications.

item.title: FoldX interface ΔΔG depends on which structure it starts from, and a learned predictor does not: a cautionary analysis on glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase
item.description: FoldX and related methods are widely used to interpret missense variants, and their sensitivity to the input structure is documented: repair of the coordinates is mandatory, averaging over structural ensembles improves agreement with experiment, and the uncertainty of a FoldX folding ΔΔG has been put at roughly ±3 kcal/mol, with binding stability worse. What has not been asked is whether that uncertainty is spread evenly over a protein. We took 258 ClinVar missense variants in glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase, a homotetramer, verified every reference residue against the 1SIQ structure and computed ΔΔG for the 124 classified pathogenic. Eighteen variants were then recomputed on three molecular dynamics snapshots of the same complex: six interface variants selected on their monomer-to-tetramer difference, six interface variants drawn at random, and six at least 10 Å from any contact. The displacement between the crystal-based value and the relaxed-frame mean had a median of 1.10, 1.38 and 0.20 kcal/mol in the three groups (random interface against distant, Mann-Whitney p = 0.0130), while frame-to-frame scatter was indistinguishable between them (Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.385). The variation is therefore positional, and it is not explained by noise in the mean. SAAMBE-3D, a learned interface predictor, run on the same eighteen variants and the same four structures, moved by a median of 0.075 kcal/mol at the interface and by nothing at all away from it, so the instability is largely a property of FoldX. It also depends on magnitude: G171R, scored at +22.53 kcal/mol, moved 2.7%, whereas A421V moved from +0.18 kcal/mol, which reads as tolerated, to +4.37 ± 2.22. Along the way we found that ThermoMPNN given a chain selector on a tetramer returns values identical to the isolated monomer at all 7,800 scanned positions. For variant interpretation the consequence is specific: at a subunit interface, in the range where a classification is actually in doubt, a single starting structure does not support a single number.

item.title: Assessing the Impact of Incorporating Bias-Adjusted
item.description: Understanding global ground-level ozone is hindered by significant monitoring gaps. To address this, we introduce a Bayesian Maximum Entropy data fusion framework that includes satellite ozone observations, generating a global 0.1° surface ozone dataset (2005–2022). Satellite observations (IASI+GOME2, OMI/MLS), adjusted to ground-level estimates, were analyzed using Flexible Regionalized Air Quality Model Performance to correct biases and estimate variance. Ground observations (hard data) and satellite-derived estimates (soft data) were then integrated, 2 using a composite of 10 atmospheric chemistry models and 3 reanalyses as the global spatialtemporal trend. Cross-validations demonstrated high overall accuracy (R2 = 0.83; RMSE = 3.73 ppb). Although integrating satellite-derived soft data yields only marginal performance gains in densely monitored areas, it substantially reduces model uncertainties and improves model accuracy across large spatial gaps. Notably, for the furthest unmonitored gap group at a 20° checkerboard, including satellite data increased R2 by 25.9% and decreased RMSE by 21.1% after the integration. Applying this optimized data fusion configuration from 2005 to 2022, global population-weighted ozone is estimated to have increased by 0.21 ppb/decade. Consequently, the global population exposed to ozone levels exceeding 50 ppb more than doubled over this 18-year period, rising from 17.2% to 41.0%.

item.title: Peptide nitrile ligation enables thioester-free chemical protein synthesis
item.description: Native chemical ligation has transformed chemical protein synthesis, yet its reliance on C-terminal peptide thioesters suffers from precursor preparation, stability and multisegment assembly. Here we report peptide nitrile ligation (PNL), a thioester-free ligation in which a stable C-terminal peptide nitrile is chemoselectively captured by an N-terminal cysteine and converted through a thiazoline intermediate into a native Xaa-Cys amide bond. Peptide nitriles are generated directly and chemoselectively from the C-terminal amides obtained using conventional Rink-amide Fmoc solid-phase peptide synthesis. PNL proceeds in aqueous buffer at pH 7.5 without an exogenous thiol catalyst, a thioester intermediate or detectable epimerization at the ligation junction. Notably, PNL enables efficient ligation at C-terminal proline junctions, a longstanding challenge in thioester-based ligation, without specialized building blocks or additional synthetic steps. The reaction tolerates internal cysteine thiols and Asn- or Gln-derived side-chain nitriles, with the latter subsequently restored to their native amides. On-demand conversion of C-terminal amide into a new nitrile enables iterative three-segment assembly. PNL therefore establishes C-terminal nitriles as stable, programmable acyl donors for thioester-free multisegment peptide ligation.

item.title: Computational Interactions between the Endohedral Metallofullerene Gd@C60 and Human Toll-Like Receptor 3: A Molecular Docking and Molecular Dynamics Study
item.description: Background: Endohedral metallofullerenes (EMFs), such as the gadolinium fullerene Gd@C60, are being explored as kinetically stable alternatives to gadolinium chelate contrast agents and as platforms for nanomedicine. Their behavior in a biological medium depends strongly on how they interact with proteins. Toll-like receptor 3 (TLR3) is an endosomal receptor that senses double-stranded RNA, and it is a relevant partner because nanoparticles are commonly internalized into endosomes. How Gd@C60 might bind to human TLR3 (hTLR3) is not known. Methods: A Gd@C60 model was built by inserting Gd3+ into C60 and optimized with the universal force field. It was docked to the crystal structure of the hTLR3 ectodomain (PDB ID: 1ZIW) using the PatchDock shape-complementarity algorithm. The top-ranked complex was then simulated for 20 ns in explicit solvent (TIP3P water, 0.15 mol/L KCl) with NAMD 2.13 and the CHARMM36 force field. Results: The best-ranked docking solution (geometric complementarity score 3908) placed Gd@C60 in the C-terminal cap region of the horseshoe-shaped receptor. The pose is stabilized by π–π stacking with Trp656, electrostatic interactions with Lys627 and Arg635, and a hydrophobic contact with Ile654, all without covalent bonding. In the simulation, the receptor backbone RMSD fluctuated at about 3–5 Å, whereas the fullerene RMSD fluctuated more widely with intermittent spikes. Conclusions: Aromatic, electrostatic and hydrophobic contacts together define the predicted binding mode of Gd@C60 on hTLR3. The net charge on the cage complicates the identification of a suitable binding pocket. The results provide a starting point for quantum-mechanical and free-energy studies and for the design of nanomaterial-based sensors of nucleic acids.

item.title: Dielectric Dynamics and Polar Nanoregions in Ferroelectric Nematic Liquid Crystals of the nJK Series
item.description: This study presents a comprehensive investigation of polarization dynamics and phase transitions in a novel homologous series of polar nematics (nJK, n=1-5) using broadband dielectric spectroscopy (DS). The analysis of dielectric spectra in planar and homeotropic cells revealed the evolution of relaxation mechanisms, transitioning from single-particle molecular reorientations in the isotropic phase to complex collective dynamics across the nematic (N), intermediate (NX), and ferroelectric nematic (NF) phases. Critical soft-mode behavior was observed near the NF transition for both the longitudinal mode (m1, acting as an amplitude mode) and the high-frequency mode (m3, exhibiting phason-like characteristics), indicating strong coupling between molecular dipoles and splay fluctuations. Furthermore, fitting the dielectric permittivity to a modified Curie–Weiss law reveals a broad temperature range of relaxor-like behavior above Tc, characterized by diffuseness exponents γ ≈1.6 for ferroelectric members ( 3JK,4JK). This confirms the formation of Polar Nanoregions (PNRs) stabilized by lateral shifted molecular arrangements in the high-temperature nematic liquid, establishing a nematic relaxor ferroelectric (nRFE) state spanning almost the entire N phase window.

item.title: CoOx/Ni foam as catalyst for the electrochemical reforming of a complex ethanosolv-derived carbohydrate stream
item.description: The electrocatalytic reforming of complex carbohydrate mixtures derived from hemicellulose has broad prospects in the green production of hydrogen and high-value chemicals. In this work, a CoOx/Ni foam (NF) electrocatalyst is used to funnel a complex carbohydrate mixture, obtained from a flowthrough mild-ethanosolv fractionation, to simplified valuable organic acid salts at room temperature. The CoOx/NF catalyst was prepared using a Co9S8/NF precursor and its electrooxidation performance was studied using xylose as a model molecule. At ambient temperature and pressure, the CoOx/NF electrocatalyst is seen to significantly reduce the electrooxidation potential of xylose compared to an activated NF electrode. Moreover, CoOx/NF achieved a formate yield as high as 73% at 1.42 V vs. reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE), while with the activated NF electrode the yield was only 46%. Density functional theory calculations revealed that interfacial electron transfer in the CoOx/NF significantly enhances the adsorption of xylose, thereby effectively improving reactivity and selectivity. When the CoOx/NF catalyst is used in the electrooxidation of crude carbohydrate streams, it reduces the measured potentials compared to the oxygen evolution reaction, and effectively generates formate and oxalate. This work demonstrates an efficient and environmentally friendly strategy for upgrading biorefinery side-streams into value-added chemicals.

item.title: From Bench to Game Engine: An Instructor-Built Suite of 3D Laboratory Simulations Created with Generative AI
item.description: Virtual chemistry laboratories have historically required either a commercial subscription or a software development team, placing custom simulations out of reach for most instructors. I report the design and construction of a suite of browser-playable 3D laboratory simulations for a non-science-majors chemistry course that has no formal laboratory component — density of an unknown metal, pH of common solutions, double replacement reactions, separations by paper chromatography, and physical and chemical changes — that I built alone in the Unity game engine, with no prior game-development experience, using a large-language-model coding assistant connected directly to the engine. Each lab pairs a 3D fume hood, rendered by a Unity WebGL build, with an HTML worksheet that checks readings, assigns per-student unknowns, and prints a one-page report; the answer data lives in the compiled build rather than in the page, so students cannot read it from the source. The labs serve two purposes: laboratory experience for students who would otherwise have none, and continuity of instruction when hurricane closures disrupt the weekly schedule. I describe the development workflow, the division of labor between instructor and AI, the design decisions that keep the simulations chemically honest, the time and cost involved, and the limitations encountered. All builds, worksheet pages, and prelab reviews are freely available on GitHub. The approach offers a reproducible path for instructors to author their own laboratory simulations: the five described here were built in about one month.

item.title: Adapting UMA to spin-polarized AQCat25 without catastrophic forgetting with task-gated LoRA
item.description: Universal models for atoms such as UMA rival specialized interatomic potentials across chemistry [2], yet none of their catalysis datasets contains spin-polarized metallic surfaces [4, 9, 10]. On AQCat25 [1], a spin-polarized, higher-fidelity catalysis dataset, UMA loses accuracy where adsorption changes surface magnetization, and fine-tuning risks catastrophic forgetting [8, 13]. We add a task-specific mode to UMA through low-rank adapters (LoRA) [5] that act only on AQCat25 systems (0.065% of parameters). On unseen adsorbates and materials, the adsorption-energy error falls from 0.193 to 0.119 eV (−38%) and the force error from 0.091 to 0.031 eV/Å, with the largest gains on strongly magnetic systems. All seven original UMA tasks remain numerically unchanged, whereas full fine-tuning raised the OC20 error tenfold. EV2-in+midFiLM [3], the best model in the AQCat25 paper, reaches 0.268 eV on the same systems. Rather than predicting adsorption energies directly, UMA derives them from total energies, as the AQCat25 authors recommend for surfaces that restructure [1]. A foundation potential can thus gain a spin-aware, higher-fidelity mode without forgetting what it already knows.

item.title: Calcium Poly(heptazine imide): Reproducible Synthesis for Structural Analysis, Mechanism of CO2 Uptake, and Evaluation of Photocatalytic CO2- to-CO Conversion
item.description: The framework material, calcium poly(heptazine imide) or CaPHI, is reportedly capable for CO2 absorption, although harsh conditions from literature synthesis method result in low and unpredictable yield that hinders evaluation of its applicability for CO2 capture and conversion (CCC). This work presents a synthesis procedure for CaPHI with cross-laboratory reproducibility and scalable to 100s mg by employing a CaCl2-based eutectic as synthesis medium. Comprehensive characterization confirmed the PHI structure, with Ca2+ residing in the structural porosity having ionic conductivity of 10-10–10-11 S cm-1 as estimated by electrochemical measurements. In addition to the literature’s physisorption mechanism for dry CO2, we demonstrated these Ca2+ to participate in direct air capture of humid CO2, which chemisorbs as CaCO3 from structural analyses. For photocatalytic CO2-to-CO conversion, CaPHI outperforms its K+-bearing counterpart, which we speculatively attributed to strong Ca2+–CO2 interactions that concentrate this reactant near the active sites. In establishing a reliable synthesis and demonstrating its ability for CO2 capture and photoreduction, further optimization of CaPHI’s structure, morphology and compositing with co-catalyst could reveal its potential for CCC, while incorporation of mobile Ca2+ may represent a broad design principle warranting future research for material development for improving the efficiency of carbon capture & utilization.

item.title: Controlled Decoration of Electrochemically Exfoliated Graphene with Gold Nanoparticles for Electrocatalysis and Sensing
item.description: The controlled decoration of graphene with metal nanoparticles benefits catalysis and sensing, yet remains challenging. Here, electrochemically exfoliated graphene (EEG) is decorated with surfactant-free gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) through a simple one-pot synthesis that uses only water, sodium hydroxide and glycerol, all inexpensive and green reagents. The AuNPs grow directly on the graphene surface. Base concentration governs particle size, whereas the Au/EEG ratio controls loading with only minor changes in size, allowing the two parameters to be tuned almost independently. The resulting composite reaches an Au loading of 20 wt%, to our knowledge among the highest reported for surfactant-free AuNPs on EEG. In the ethanol oxidation reaction, it outperformed physically mixed, sequentially deposited and ligandstabilized controls, combining the highest mass activity with the lowest Tafel slope and the largest electrochemically active surface area. As a proof-of-concept tryptophan sensor, it oxidized the analyte at 0.57 V, to our knowledge the lowest overpotential reported for this amino acid, with a linear response from 1 to 100 µM, a detection limit of 0.4 µM and good tolerance to common electroactive interferents. This strategy offers a scalable, green platform for printable catalysts and sensors.

item.title: Elucidating permselectivity mechanisms in polyamide membranes through controlled chlorination and hydrolysis
item.description: Polyamide membranes are widely used in freshwater production because of their high water permeance and water–salt selectivity, but emerging applications require tunable permselectivity. We investigate the structure–property–performance relationships governing membrane behavior by modifying permselectivity through sequential chlorination and alkaline treatment. Chemical, structural, and transport properties are examined using X-ray characterization, free-energy barrier analysis, and molecular dynamics simulations. We find chlorine–alkaline modification more than doubles water permeance through hydrolysis, which enhances swelling, increases water–membrane interactions, and promotes water transport. Despite the resulting looser structure, the hydrolyzed membrane maintains water–salt selectivity because of entropic barriers to salt transport, likely caused by the presence of bulky chlorine groups on the aromatic rings. These findings identify distinct mechanisms by which chemical modification alters water and salt transport, challenge the prevailing view that swelling is detrimental to selectivity, and provide new design insights for tuning polyamide membrane performance.

item.title: Conformational Dynamics of Cation-Cryptophane Complexes by Ion Mobility Mass Spectrometry
item.description: Cryptophanes can selectively encapsulate small molecules and cations. Tuning host-guest selectivity requires insight into molecular recognition, which is analytically accessible with ion mobility mass spectrometry (IM-MS) via the conformational dynamics of complexation. Using activated IM-MS to differentiate between encapsulated and externally associated species, anti-cryptophanes complexes of the cation H+, Li+, Na+, K+, Rb+, Cs+, Mg2+, and Ag+ were investigated. The m/z of fragments are characteristic of the binding mode of the host and guest pair. Using the combination of characteristic m/z and changes in ion mobility, IM-MS was sensitive to the host’s binding mode and provided further support to whether encapsulation had taken place. These findings demonstrate that activated IM-MS can sensitively probe cryptophane binding modes and provide new insight into the selectivity of cation encapsulation.

item.title: Ten-Step Total Synthesis of the Octadride (+)-Zopfiellin via Electrochemical Decarboxylative Cross-Coupling
item.description: We report the first asymmetric total synthesis of the antifungal octadride natural products zopfiellin and deoxyzopfiellin. Our highly convergent synthetic strategy features a bioinspired electrochemical nickel-catalyzed decarboxylative cross-coupling of two readily available fragments to assemble the core skeleton. This key transformation enables a subsequent intramolecular alkylation, forging the eight-membered carbocycle with excellent diastereoselectivity. Notably, the protecting-group-free route is robust and scalable, providing access to (+)-zopfiellin in 10 steps.

item.title: Wigner Momentum Estimation and Sampling with Local Modes: A Second-Moment Approximation to High-Frequency Momentum Marginals
item.description: Instantaneous local Gaussian approximations assign nuclear momentum widths from the curvature of the potential at each sampled configuration. Strongly compressed bonds can consequently acquire large momentum widths even when their positions are drawn from an anharmonic path-integral ensemble. We estimate momentum covariances from pathintegral coordinates and forces in local modes that follow molecular deformations. These covariances define Gaussian approximations to high-frequency Wigner momentum marginals without evaluating a Hessian at each configuration. The resulting sampling recovers the Maxwell momentum distribution in the classical limit. A rotating bond model with harmonic stretching and periodic torsion agrees with an independent quantum reference within statistical uncertainty. For trans-azobenzene at 300 K with 32 beads, the most compressed C–H bond receives a mass-weighted momentum variance of 36.53 kJ mol−1 from LGA and 19.55 kJ mol−1 from the local covariance along the same physical stretch direction. Temporal holdout errors in C–H second moments are 7.2–7.6%, compared with 2.2–5.1% for LGA relative to the finite-bead reference; the demonstrated benefit concerns the suppression of local width spikes. The largest collective C–H width remains sensitive to estimator noise. These results support the method as an approximation to high-frequency momentum widths without a frequency cap. Position-conditioned quantum correlations, non-Gaussian tails, and the continuum-bead molecular limit remain outside the demonstrated accuracy.

item.title: Explainable Graph Neural Networks Reveal Molecular Features Associated with Umami Taste
item.description: Umami is one of the five basic tastes, and understanding the relationship between molecular structure and umami perception is important for food science. Although machine learning models have been developed to predict umami taste, the molecular features underlying their predictions remain insufficiently understood. In this study, we developed a graph neural network (GNN) model for umami taste prediction and investigated the structural features contributing to its predictions using Integrated Gradients (IG). Three datasets were constructed from ChemTastesDB, comprising 74 umami compounds and different sets of non-umami compounds. Under five-fold Murcko scaffold-disjoint cross-validation, the model achieved mean receiver operating characteristic areas under the curve of 0.935, 0.950, and 0.910 for the strict, full primary, and physicochemically matched datasets, respectively. Atom-level IG analysis revealed that functional-group prevalence did not necessarily correspond to positive attribution toward umami prediction. Notably, carboxylic acids occurred at similar frequencies in umami and non-umami compounds but showed significantly greater positive attribution in umami compounds. Furthermore, analysis of 31 structurally similar umami–nonumami molecular pairs demonstrated that regions specific to umami compounds generally received greater positive attribution than the corresponding regions in non-umami compounds. These findings suggest that the GNN captures molecular features associated with umami taste in a manner that depends on their surrounding structural context. Combining scaffold-disjoint prediction with atom-level attribution analysis provides an approach for investigating structure–taste relationships and identifying molecular features potentially relevant to umami perception.

item.title: Quantitative Protein–Ligand Binding Affinity Prediction from Quantum-Mechanical Scoring
item.description: Quantitative prediction of protein–ligand (P–L) binding affinities is generally thought to require extensive configurational sampling, which is computationally demanding. Here, we examine how closely a fundamentally different approach, a quantum-mechanical (QM) description of P–L binding energetics based on a small set of representative structures, can approach the accuracy of MD-based free-energy calculations. Large-scale validation of the SQM2.20 scoring function is carried out on the Public Free Energy Benchmark data set, comprising 88 P–L series with 1,113 ligands in total. To compare directly with the experimental binding free energies (∆Gbind), a scaling factor derived independently in the PL-REX data set was applied, yielding SQM2.20sc. With refined receptor structures and an extended pool of ligand poses, SQM2.20sc achieved a weighted pairwise root-mean-square error (RMSE) in ∆∆G of 1.41 kcal/mol, close to the 1.26 kcal/mol reported for FEP+. n a subset of 58 targets and 872 ligands, SQM2.20sc (RMSE 1.41 kcal/mol) outperformed OpenFE (1.74 kcal/mol). These results demonstrate the transferability of the approach across a wide range of protein targets and ligand chemistries, further strengthening the case for SQM scoring as a computationally efficient tool for applications in computer-aided drug design.

item.title: Photocatalytic Reductive Elimination From A Main Group Centre
item.description: The development of “transition metal-like” reactivity using earth-abundant p-block elements is one of the most prominent and challenging goals of contemporary main group chemistry. This difficulty is exemplified by the key, catalytically relevant bond-forming step of reductive elimination which, while often facile for transition metals, is very difficult to achieve for most main group elements. Efforts to bridge this gap have typically focused on delicate tailoring of electronic structure, supporting ligands, and coordination geometry, a task that is conceptually difficult and synthetically demanding. Herein, we demonstrate an alternative approach. We show that photocatalytic reductive elimination from an already well-known P(V) complex can be achieved rapidly and under mild conditions, via a transient oxidation strategy analogous to “oxidatively induced reductive elimination”. This concept has previously been applied only to transition metal complexes but is now extended to the field of main group chemistry. These results demonstrate a simple, easily accessible, but potentially very powerful new strategy for ‘turbocharging’ transition metal-like reactivity at a main group centre. Thus, it provides a valuable new tool for the ongoing pursuit of transition metal-like catalysis using main group elements.

item.title: Structural Basis for Nitrile-Directed Recognition of the Catalytic Lysine in KIT
item.description: KIT and PDGFRA are the major oncogenic drivers in gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GIST). Although clinically approved KIT/PDGFRA-directed tyrosine kinase inhibitors (such as imatinib and avapritinib) have improved patient outcomes, long-term efficacy is often limited by additional resistance mutations in these kinases. To explore alternative interaction modes less susceptible to mutational escape, we investigated the catalytic lysine K623 in KIT as an anchoring point for inhibitor design. Starting from avapritinib, we prepared nitrile-containing analogues in which the canonical pyrimidine core was replaced by a nitrile-substituted aromatic scaffold. The compounds were evaluated biochemically against KIT and the closely related GIST driver PDGFRA, including clinically relevant mutant forms, and were further assessed in cellular models of PDGFRA-driven GIST. Co-crystal structures revealed a distinct binding mode in which the nitrile group is directed toward K623, reorienting the ligand within the ATP-binding site while retaining kinase inhibitory activity. Guided by these structural findings, electrophilic analogues bearing squaric ester warheads were developed to probe covalent target engagement. Intact-protein mass spectrometry demonstrated time-, concentration-, and pH-dependent covalent labeling of KIT, with complete mono-labeling of the detectable soluble protein population observed under near-physiological conditions. Pre-occupation of the ATP-binding site with either avapritinib or a covalent ATP-site binder selectively suppressed the earliest and kinetically favored labeling event, supporting an active-site-dependent component of covalent modification. Together, these results establish the catalytic lysine K623 as a structurally accessible interaction site in KIT and show that this binding geometry can provide a basis for proximity-driven covalent kinase targeting.

item.title: Fragment-Grounded Neural Simulation of Electron Ionization Mass Spectra at Library Scale
item.description: Electron ionization mass spectrometry (EI-MS) is a sensitive, reproducible analytical technique, yet compound identification conventionally relies on reference databases that capture only a fraction of accessible chemical space. In silico prediction of EI-MS spectra can extend these libraries, but existing data-driven models generalize poorly beyond their training distribution, and physics-based simulations are too costly for library-scale use. Here, we present a fragment-grounded neural workflow that predicts an EI-MS spectrum by exhaustively enumerating the fragmentation graph of a molecule and then assigning intensities to the resulting substructures. By relating every predicted peak back to a candidate substructure, our model generalizes more reliably to unseen scaffolds and out-of-distribution chemistry than prior fingerprint-and black-box transformer-based predictors. On a scaffold split, it improves top-1 retrieval accuracy from formula-matched compounds by 32% relative to the strongest baseline, and it matches the accuracy of quantum-chemical simulation while being roughly seven orders of magnitude faster. To test the model’s capabilities under a harder, formula-agnostic setting, we further evaluate retrieval against a library of 87.3 million compounds from

item.title: Activity-based Detection of MUTYH using Engineered Dumbbell DNA Switches
item.description: Transitioning from quantitative abundance measurements to functional activity-based assays represents a key opportunity in DNA repair research, particularly for enzymes like MUTYH that currently lack functional assay platforms. Here, we developed a FRET-based DNA switch for real-time monitoring of MUTYH glycosylase activity. The dumbbell-like architecture incorporates an 8-oxoG: A mismatch that leads to structure switching upon MUTYH-mediated adenine excision, resulting in activity-dependent fluorescence signal change. We demonstrate that the rationally designed GC-rich DNA nanoswitch can detect both E. coli MutY and human MUTYH with high specificity, enabling real-time activity monitoring directly in bacterial free cell extracts. In addition, the assay can be easily adapted for inhibitor screening, demonstrating its potential for drug screening applications. The activity-based assay was also implemented in HeLa cells and analyzed by confocal microscopy, confirming preferential localization of the MUTYH activity within the nuclear compartment. Overall, this simple, low-cost DNA-based sensor bridges the need for functional assays by directly monitoring MUTYH glycosylase activity in complex biological environments, offering a scalable platform for future screening applications.

item.title: Understanding the Relationship Between Synthetic Conditions and H2 Uptake Capacity in Oxidatively Activated Turbostratic Carbons through Machine Learning
item.description: The relationship between synthesis parameters, porosity, and H2 uptake in activated carbons is a field of significant investigation and discussion. Conclusions about these relationships are typically drawn from limited datasets of carbons produced for a given publication, and are not able to consider the interplay between various synthesis parameters and properties of the resultant turbostratic carbons. We present the first attempt at understanding the relationship between synthesis parameters and H2 uptake capacity in turbostratic carbons, using the single point pore volume as a proxy due to the dearth of available high pressure H2 isotherms. The methods used herein have exploited a dataset of 237 samples to determine the most important synthesis parameters in determining the porosity of the product and thus their suitability for high pressure H2 storage applications.

item.title: Random Copolymerization of L-Lactide with Six-membered Cyclic Oxalates Enables Simultaneous Toughening and Tunable Degradation of Poly(L-lactic acid)
item.description: Poly(L-lactic acid) (PLLA) is one of the most important biobased and biodegradable polyesters, but its intrinsic brittleness and slow degradation in natural environments still hamper its extensive applications. Developing PLLA materials that combine high strength and toughness with tunable degradation behavior remains a significant challenge. In this contribution, we present the bulk ring-opening copolymerization (ROCP) of L-lactide (L-LA) with each of three six-membered cyclic oxalates (sAOx), namely ethylene oxalate (EOx), 1,2-propylene oxalate (POx) and 1,2-hexylene oxalate (HOx), to produce a series of P(LLA-co-sAOx) statistical copolyesters using Sn(Oct)2 as the catalyst. The P(LLA-co-POx) statistical copolyesters exhibited the most favorable strength–toughness balance. At a POx content of 15 mol%, the P(LLA-co-POx) copolyester exhibited an elongation at break of 224% and a toughness of 63.7 MJ m-3 while retaining a high yield strength of 50.3 MPa. This toughness was approximately 33 times that of neat poly(L-lactide) (PLLA). In addition, the P(LLA-co-POx) statistical copolyesters exhibited good barrier performance and showed potential application as packaging materials. More importantly, the incorporation of POx endowed the copolyesters with excellent degradability and composition-dependent degradation behavior under natural environmental conditions. The P(LLA-co-POx) copolyester with a POx content of 50 mol% completely degradation within 80 days in soil. This work provides a chemical modification strategy for designing high-performance and sustainable PLLA-based packaging materials.

item.title: Side-Chain Structure Reprograms Helical Folding in Isotactic Oligourethanes
item.description: Sequence-defined abiotic polymers could extend the structural organization underlying biological function to new backbones and operating environments, but this requires rules connecting monomer structure to folding. Predictive control over folding is essential for translating molecular information into defined structure and, ultimately, function. Here, we show that side-chain structure reprograms the conformational landscape of isotactic oligourethanes. A systematic series of isotactic tetramers bearing structurally diverse substituents was examined by circular dichroism, two-dimensional nuclear magnetic resonance, and Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy, supported by molecular dynamics simulations. Side chains that combine effective backbone shielding with steric compatibility favor persistent 2.614-helical states in competitive polar media, whereas less compatible substituents populate broader, dynamically interconverting helical ensembles. Notably, side-chain substitution can reverse the chiroptical bias of an invariant SSSS-configured backbone, reflecting a change in the preferred helical handedness. Experiments and simulations further reveal that helix persistence is associated with the interplay of reduced solvent exposure of the polar backbone, steric compatibility within the folded geometry, and recurrent intramolecular hydrogen bonding. The results establish side-chain selection as a means of directing oligourethane folding without changing backbone stereochemistry and identify complementary molecular criteria for developing scaffold-specific folding rules.

item.title: Self-assembly of DNA-β-sheet peptide conjugates into emergent micrometer-sized rods
